div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

The Duchess of York left on Wednesday evening for White Lodge, Richmond Park, where the most interesting event of the year is expected to take place about the middle of the month. Dr. Williams, who owes his selection to the Princess Beatrice, takes an exceedingly encouraging view of the manner in which the Duchess is keeping up her strength,

Mrs. John Strange Winter tells a good story of Air. Frank Lockwood, whose ready wit is well known and widely admired by all classes in London. He was going to a big reception one evening, when he happened to hear the gentleman passing in jut in front of him give his name to the servant thus— after the common custom of taking the name from the land, which obtains in bonny Scotland—" The Glen-Muish and Mrs. McKenzie." Quick as thought Mr. Lockwood.whl came next, gave his name to the man as "15, Portland Place and Mrs. Lockwood."

Some amusement has been caused by Nr. Cham- berlain's eulogy of the member fcr North Padding- ton, and his doubtless innocent attempt to make capital out of Lord Randolph leaving a safe seat to fight Central Bradford. Now, as a matter of fact, he has done no such thing, but has obtained per- mission from the Conservative Committee of the division to oppose Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, while still re- taining his present seat,where he will be unopposed. The whole affair is a little party move to resusci- tate falling popularity, and certainly involves no sacrifice.

The latest issue of the Lee-let ford rifle illus- trates the improvements that. have been made as the result of the recent experiments. The " feed" of the cartridges has been so. improved that the magazine will take ten instead of eight, the barrel has been lightened, the sight is now graduated tth to eighteen hundred yards, and the total average weight has been reduced to nine pounds four ounces. The experts have reported to the War Office that the effect of these improvements is to considerably increase the effectiveness of the weapon and to still further establish its claim to being the best army rifle in use in Europe.

In these days of fierce competition, dearth of work, decreasing incomes. and increased extrava- gance it is likely that Sir John Lubbock will shortly possess a rival in his Parliamentary canonization in the person of Mt. A. J. Williams, M.P. That is it the latter is able to carry his Jury Law Amend- ment Bill. A new and well paid profession will be opened to the needy. It will give fifteen shillings a day to merchants and professional men, seven shillings and sixpense to shopkeepers and farmers, six shillings to artisAns, and four shillings to labourers, with travelling expenses. of course. And for special jurors it lays down a definite standard of qualification.

The most striking thing about the House of Com- mons on Wednesday afternoon was the fact, re- vealed by the divi,ion taken just after four o'clock, that, there were :337 members in attendance on Derby clay. But, just as it is one thing to lead a horse to the water and quite another to make him drink, so it was found far easier to keep a phalanx of members in attemlance at Wesrmitpter than to induce them to listen to the abstruse and technical disquisitions of lawyers and statists on the taxable properties of settled estates. The gloom of the afternoon was deepened by the air of martyrdom that. pervaded the assembly, and by unmistakable manifestations that, their hearts were not, in the death rates, but at Epson.

The lamentable cab strike has brought to light the fact that there is an aristocracy even in the ranks of hackney-carriage Jehus. Yet, among this aristocracy there is one who, like a few—a very few .—of the aristocracy of birth, does not allow his exalted station to interfere with the dictates of his heart, lie is out on strike out of pure sympathy For his fellows. This driver. who is orpe of the very fortunate Jell us of the metropoliz, has not to "crawl" along the streets or take up his po,ition at a cab-stand, but has quite a dczen regular engage- ments a day, and in tile evening has often the plea- sure of driving such men as lr Henry Irving home after the theatres are closed. Yet he nas renounced his lucrative little business for the time being., and taken to collecting pence fof the strike fund.

The great race at Ere,om, which was once more run on Wednesday, has been run for 114 years; but for a considerable time before that there were small local race meetings on the Downs, which were occaslons of much le-qivity among the sporting people of the country round. In 1780 the Lord Derby of the flay, a keen sportsman, made hitn-elf the patron of the meeting, and the principal race of the day.in which he had horses running, was named after him. From that year it has borne the same name, and it will probably bear it for anoth‘r hun- dred years to come. In its earlier years the race drew very few Londoners to Epsom outside the ranks of the sporting gentry, but. as the reputation of the meeting increased, it spread !rom society to the ma-4ses, and at last became a kind of notional gathering. The sister race, the Oaks, took its name from an estst of the same Lord Derby, which was siteated close to Epsom nowns. Epsom itself was a romantic IP tie village, patronised by Royalty and fashion, and its water, gave it the character of a spa, at whose fountain, and in whose pure air, the fashionable hypochondriac and invalid sought health.

It would be interesting to know how Lord Rose- liery came to give his horse a name so much out of the common, so classical and yet so little, known that Echotars have been hunting through the Latin poets and the classical dictionaries to fliscov •r its origin. The Provost of Eton is not the onl v one ,who has been to his bookshelf to search not the classic cognomen. According to the master of Lord Rosebery's sables his lordship cannot pronounce the name if his own horse, at least not to.satisfy the ear of his chief stableman. But the public will rather take his lordship's Scotch sound of the Latin vowel than the On dint of the good old Scot of 75 who presides over his raccrs and probably never had a Latin grammar in his hand. The original Ladas was a great runner of antiquity, and was in the service of Alexander the Great. lie too, once 'carried off a great prize, the first at Olympia, for his royal master. lie died, however, in the moment of victory ; whereas the Premier's horse will live to enjoy his laurels and his oats, and to he indifferent to politics. Nor is the protost of Etoes line in Juvenal the only reference to the Swift runner in the writers of antiquity.

It is now of course certain that, the Government will carry the death 'duties portion of their Budget scheme without difficulty. But on the other hand, it is becoming more and more probable that. the division on the additional whisky duty will be ef critical character, and the Government will have to make every effort to ensure a full'muster of their supporters. Of course it is kno.vn that—apart from the action of the Parnellites—certain English Lib- erals who are interested in " the trade " cannot he relied upon to support this part of the Budget Bill as they are supporting the others. It has been, hitherto, however, generally assumed that the Gov- ernment could count on Phtaininvr the votes, or at I all events being helped by the abstention, of some of the Unionist absentees. It, is now placed beyond doubt, that if they rely upon thiq they will be trust- ing to a broken reed. I have direct authority for saying that Mr. William Johnston and Mr. T. W. RuSsell, two of the Unionists whose names have hen most. freely mentioned in this connection,have made up their minds to put their Unionism before their teetotalism and vote against the Government. So, no doubt, it will be with any other possible waverers. The Unionist Whips, lam told, are of opinion that the Government cannot count on a majority of more than seven or eight ; and it. is evident. that if this is the case, and if any of the Liberals should by accident he absent impaired— and on the eve of a great division accident 3 have always to be guarded against—the voting may be. very close indeed. The most. favourablecalcnlation I have heard only puts the majority at twelve. When once the divisions on the whisky and beer duty are over all will be plain sailing as far as the Budget is concerned.

Telezr.m. from Victoria ;tate that 100,000 acre. of the hest land in British Columbia are under water. The rainfall has been extraordinarily heavy, and the Fraser River has tecome a vast lake, extending for hundreds of miles.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER
hilr. DEAREST NE LLI E,

The millinery of the year is truly egregious. ss bonnet with -violet velvet crown is trimmed with red berries. Another in sickly pink straw is trimmed with green velvet and scarlet geraniums, this latter blossom being in high favour at the moment. A third has a pretty enough little gar- land of wateroress leaves about the brim, but their refreshing suggestion of coolness is thwarted by the truly tetrible crowd of mingle] red, pink, and yellow roses, all in livid and grotesque tones of colour, that is massed upon the crown. These aberrations are probably short-lived, or the san- guine are hoping so. A peculiarly brilliant tone of green is one of the worst sinners In this respect, It is called " aquatic," but it is more suggestive of the old bright arsenic green than of anything in the domain of Neptune. It is seen in straw, and is said to be in preparation for dress materials. Only a negress, or a Hindoo, however, could wear such a brilliant tint with impunity. A charming bonnet is made of bLick. chip with strings of resdia green watered riVon and rosettes of the same decking the front, together with some bows of black chip and an assertive-looking black bird. The entire crown is formed of Valenciennes lace, and a bunch of multi coloured clover is arranged to rest on the hair at the back.

In the very newest coat and skirt style for the season are the orthodox black moire Idea yes and black moire revers, while the skirt shows a deep hem of the same trimming, and the waistcoat itself is remarkably prominent from the fact that it is of shiny satin, carefully covered with a coarse make of saffron-tinted lace. The material of which the costume is made is dark grey cloth, and the satin waistcoat may be of any shade, the brighter the better, so that it prove sufficiently becoming to the wearer. Among the fashionable shades are mauve, apple-green, and old-rose, while a lovely shade of orange is creeping into favour, but this colour needs careful wearing, and I can only recommend it with dark hair and a perfectly clear complexion. Even then it will need covering with black lace, so per- haps you will consider so sombre a waistcoat hardly seasonable.

Moire is very popular for separate bodices, and the new zauave bodices in moire completely cover the baEque to the waist, and fit closely, and long sash ends and loops fall from the waist point. The fronts are rounded off, and connected over the bsut with a large flat bow. This is a very useful kind of top, and may be worn over a sleeveless vest and skirt en suite, as the zouave has large full sleeves of the moire. Most of tho capes have a bow in front, and a goodly number of the new blouses are completed in a similar fashion. Tuseore silk is in much requisi- tion for Blouses, as complying with the general fancy for "fresh-butter" colour, as well as being convenient as a tint that can be worn with any other. Tusores, or "tussahs" are made in a variety of fancy patterns, some with a pin•spot, some with a satin star, and others with a delicate floral stripe. An admirable cape of its kind which has come under my notice is made of moire with a deep collar round the neck contrived into revers In the front, and is outlined with a narrow edging of 6Jru embroidery.

Although plain skirts will be wcrn this summer, yet the newest style is undoubtedly the draped skirt; and in the front arrangements these cer- tainly resemble the draped gowns worn some years back. With the old draped skirts, the bustle; or dress-improver, was a very palpable fact, and enlarged the figure and gave& broader and rounder reappearance; but the present skirts are kept small and compact at the top, and the back is quite flat, an altogether more becoming style to the figure. The basque will prevail this summer on almost popular blouses, judging by all pre- monitory signs, and instead of Victorian collars and frilled revers or graduated bretelles, the bodice part will be trimmed in various styles, and any collar or frills will be of a somewhat flatted Yours lovingly, JENS'S.

Mdme. Belle Cole had arrived in Melbourne when the last mail left, to fulfil her engagement to give forty con- certs in Australia let five thousand pounds and all ex- penses paid. The voyage from London in a fast Orient liner she describes as " a delightful trip," the first real holiday she has had for many years. Mrs. Sarah Thomas, of Barryport, South Wales.began life in 1738, and this fact having been communicated to the Princess of Wales, together with a photograph of the old lady of one hundred and six, a graceful reply was sent through Colonel Ciark:—" Her Royal High- ness is much interest:A tl hear of this very old subject of Her Majesty, and wishes to make her a little present of one hundred and six shillings, one for each birthday she has passed."

Antoinette Sterling is becoming a familiar figure upon the platform at the great temperance meetings. She speaks sometimes, though not at any great length ; most iften her speech is merely a brief introduction to her song. On these occasions she usually sings without any accompaniment. It is very interesting to see the great singer come forward so simply, as she does,quietly dressed, with no music in her hand,at one of the packed Exeter Hall meetings, and lift her beautiful voice, hold- ing the dense throng breathless with attention. Coming as an interlude in impassioned speaking, to the excited crowd the effect is unusually delightful.

div.head: Spring Work : Washing B:ankets.
div.p: Spring Work : Washing B:ankets.

Second to no other deparment of li-ousehold management is the care ot the bed-clothing, and no part of the spring work is more important than the washing of the blan- kets that have becu used through the winter, and wid be required as the best covering through the summer. In oruer to wash blankets properly, several things are necessary. A good clear day should be chosen for the work, plenty of rain water in readiness, and good soap used. It is best to have two women employed to do this washing, as one cannot very well handle large blankets. The coloured ribbons used to bind the edges very often run when wet, thus spotting and streaking them ; it is therefore best to rip them off and r,place them with a lute binding, or the edges may be ileMllled. Blankets, if left in pairs as they are usually bought, should be cut apart betow washing, as they will be much easier to handle. When ready to begin the woik, made a strong suds by dissolving the soap in a tub ot hot water, of a temperature,that may be borne by the hands, put in two or three blankets and let stand a few minutes, then dip them up and down in the water, squeezing and pressing the suds from them. Have ready another tub of clean warm suds, into which transfer the blankets, and wash as before. When they are clean, put into a tub of warn, clear water to free from the suds,then rinse in tepid blue water. Care must he taken to have all the waters the same temperature, and to be sure no soap is left in the blankets. A wringer loosened seas not to press hard may be used, but two pair of hands will do the wringing much more satisfactorily, as the blankets should be pulled and shaken more than wrung. When ready to bang out, they should bewspread eeruiy on the iine and stretched occasionally while drying. When dry, fold and place under a 'weight instead of ironing. Several elas airing may be given blankets after being washed, and to be packed away for the summer, they should be sewed up in an old cloth to protect them from moth. It is tot necessary, as some housekeepers deem it, to wash blan- kets twice a year, even if not, soiled. Instead, they niay be shaken and hung on the line for several days, to be cleaned by t• e sun and wind quite as effectively as if washed.

Giraida spring fr-orn her chafe glowing with joy, and approaching the old marquis, her violet eyes dewed with tears. " Then I will be your granddaughter!" she said, her voice trembling with grateful joy. "I will live with vou, and do my best to make you happy ! And—and," she added, "I will love you! I do love you now, Lord Trevelyau, for your great k ind ness." Shc stood before him, trembling and blushing, for a single moment, and then, obeying hergrateful impulse, she came closer to him and dropped a shy, fluttering kiss upon his forehead. She was astonished at the result of her childlike and innocent caress. The tears sprang to Lord Trevelyan's eyes, and his face was convulsed as with sudden anguish. No one had given him n a kiss for many years. Giralda's pure and dewy caress brought back to him the childish kisses of the boy who had slept in his bcsom—whose supposed wickedness had broken his heart. "Child with the eyes I love," he whispered, "from this moment you and I are bound together with a tie which can never be broken." He drew her to him gently, and pressed upon her forehead a fatherly, reverent kiss—a caress that was the seal to their new relations. "I will sde your mother when we go up to town," said Lord Trevelyan. "I will look for her in the theatres' and she shall accompany us to see your father. I must see Rupert and Fay, to. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON
VISIT OF THE REV. THOMAS WAUGH.

This well-known Wesleyan evangelist preached at Bewsev-road Wesleyan Chapel on Monday afternoon and evening. 't here were good congregations at both ser- • vices, more particularly at the evening service- The preacher in his sermon in the evening impressed upon tuo hearers the importance of early decision tor Christ, and pointed out that religion was not merely a thing for people to die with. Collections were taken at both ser- vices in aid of the Sankey Bridges school funds. WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The usual meeting of this society was held on Sunday afternoon, and was largely attended. Mr. G. Walling- ton presided and took as his subject " Play the man.' He referred to the occasion on which Latimer used these words, and said it had been his pleasure the previous week to stand on the spot, at Oxford, where they were spoken. He impressed upon his hearers their duty of playing the man. Cquncillor Luckinan, of Salford, • delivered the address and spoke on " Man." He referred to the many achievements of man, and to the many senses with which he was endowed. He denied that man was a creature of circumstances, and called upoa his hearers to exercise the powers they possessed, and to bring credit noon the country to which they belonged. Mrs. S. W. Jeffery sang as a solo "Shall we gather at the River," and an oboe solo " Behold and See," from the Messiah, was contributed by Mi. Ward. Mr. W. H. Payton accompanied on the organ. Messrs. A. Lang and J. Hawthorn also took part in the meeting. CAIRO-STREEr SUNDAY SCHOOL.—ANNIVERSARY

div.head: SERVICES.
div.p: SERVICES.

There were large congregations at the anniversary services in connection with Cairo-st. Sunday school, oa Sunday. The church had been decorated for the occa- sion with a choice collection of flowers and plants. Special hymns and anthems were sung, the singing of the scholars at the afternoon service being particu!arly good. The pulpit at the morning service was occupied by the pastor, the Rev. W. H. Drummond, 8.A., who preached an excellent discourse. The choir under the conductor- ship of Mr. J. M. Muir. A.C.0., sang the anthem "Blessed are the Merciful" (Hiles). Mr. Smith Knowles of Manchester, delivered an address to parents and scholars at the afternoon children's service. Mr. Henry Wright conducted the staging. At the evening service, the Rev: Charles Roper, 8.A., of Moss Side, was the preacher. The choir excellently sang the anthem " 0 Love the Lord " (Sullivan). Collections weie taken at each service in aid of the school funds and realised almost -L2O.

BEV. FATHER WRAY'S FAREWELL. At St. Mars's Roman Catholic Church on Sunday the Rev. Father Wray, who has been appointed Rector of the parish of St. Michael, Abergavenny, Monmouthshire. • referred to his approaching departure. Be remarked that during his labours among them he had had the- honour of working with two gent'emen for whom he en- - tort ained the very highest respect and regard—Father Sumner as rector of the mission and Father Duggan as fellow•assistant—and he wished to declare publicly that they had laboured together in the greatest concord and harmony. It had been a pleasure ti work under One and with the other. He left them both with regret, for a brother who was helped by a brother was like is strong tower, and he begged to thank them publicly for the great Kindness he had ever received from their hands. He was also leaving a congregation among which he Ip..d made many frit nds, and he thought, net a single enemy, .and he wished to bear testimony to the kindness and for- • bearance they had shown him, perhaps in d,fticult time F.. lie had also 40 thank the clergy of St. Alban's and many in Warrington who were not Catholics, but who had been very IrAid to him. Be was going to a place where there was a beautiful church, good schools, and a nice congregation, but he had made so many friends at Sr. - Mary's that he would rather remain among them. Ho had done all in his power to gct the decision of Ins superiors altered, but without avail, and he was obliged to leave them and take up new duties far away from the parish he had loved so much. He had hrard that many would call upon him to say " good--bye," but lie aslied them to refrain and let him go away quietly, as such an ordeal would only accentuate the pain he felt at parting from them, and, he was sure, would prove tf,o much for lum. He asked them all to remember him in their prayers, as lie Would remember them. The rev... gentleman's voice was scarcely audible with einoticn.• and many of the congregation were visibly affected. Th COMMITTEH MITTEH; PROPOSED ISOLATION HOSPITAL 111iIICt'S minutes contained a resolution to
The

the effect that the Town Clerk be requested to communi- cate with the adjoining autherities with a view to com- bined action for the establishment of a permanent isola- tion hospital, and report to the committee at its next meeting, and that the Hospital Sub-Com:nittee be re- quested to report upon the most desirable places near the borough as sites for a small-pox hospital. Alderman SUTTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the committee alluded to the nuisance caused by the condition of the river at Wilderspool, and said it would soon be abated, as the Ship Canal Company had already commenced to open the dam at Walton in order that the tide might flow into the disused portion of the Mersey. That would remedy the evil complained of. With regard to the proposed permanent isolation hospi- tal, it was well known that they were well situated in Warrington for getting the benefit of diseases imported from other towns. Warrington was also accused of being the cause of the spread of infectiou3 diseases in other towns. However, it, was pleasing to note that there had been no further spread of the smallpox, which had been recently brought into the town by a band of Italians. The spread of the disease had been arrested. It was hoped that before long a permanent hospital would be erected, either in or mear Warrington. Councillor noon seconded the motion. Councillor TINSLEY expressed a hope that the com- mittee would deal with the river nuisance with a firm hand. _ . . _

Alderman FRANCOMB observed that a deputation from the Council had already been to the spot where opera- tions with regard to the cutting away of the dam at Walton were proceeding. The work woulc.l be completed in about another week; and the horrible stench from the river would be abated. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON wished to know if it were correct that the committee were responsible for the greater portion of the nuisance, and that the Ship Canal deputation were informed of that fact the other day? Councillor ROBERTS : The Health Committee are not responsible for the greater part of the nuisance, hardly for any portion at all. A very insignificant portion are we responsible for, or is the borough responsible for. It is not true that such a statement was made to the directors at 'the recent Ship Canal meeting at the Town Hall. Councillor Bovrow : lam glad to hear that. I didn't know you were chairman of the meeting. Couucillor ROBERTS : I was not the chairman, but I was present at the meeting, and had a great deal to do with what took place. I heard all that was said, and I am, therefore, in a position ta give a fiat contradiction to the statement which has just been made. Alderman SUTTON : The committee as soon as they were aware of the nuisance took the necessary proceed- ings through the Town Clerk for the abatement of the nuisance, who intimated that it must be stopped or that legal proceedings would be taken. The Ship Canal Com- pany immediately complied with the demands which were made upon them. (Hear, hear.)
, The minutes were adopied. SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE.

The confirmation of the minutes was moved by Coun- cillor MONKS and Councillor BEAMAN. Councillor WOODS and Councillor SIIAVir each took ex- ception to the resolution of the c')mmittee in which they would not undertake to remove trade refuse. Councillor MONKS said that that innocent resolution was merely intended to refer to seven or eight people in the town,who were carrying on manufacturing business in the process of which certain refuse had been collected hitherto at the expense of the Corporation through the Sanitary Works Committee. It hardly seemed fair that such should be the case,and the committee were putting themselves in order by passing this resolution. The minutes were passed unanimously. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

Alderman WitIGIIT, in moving the adoption of the minutes of this committee, said that they would notice that the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor would wait upon the County Surveyor to discuss the subject of the maintenance of the Latchford and Wilderspool Cause- way,and also the widening f Warrington bridge. When they had done uo they would bring the matter b.;:fore the Council. Alderman BCTCIIINSON . seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were passed unanimously.

The MAYOR pr posed the adoption of the Markets Com- mittee's minutes. He said that he was sorry that there was a decrease in the receipts of this year of • £l4 17s. 61, compared with last year.. It was really time something was done for the Market Hall. There was very l'ttle being done at the present time. COUnCillOr ROBERTS supported Councillor Monks' sug- gestion, and also took the opportunity to correct Cour, cillor Henherd's statement that when the question fthe purchase of a quantity of cannel was brought up,several members of the Council objected to it. Tim purchase was not objected to. The objection Was that the cannel in question had not been advertised for, and put up for tender. Councillor SMETHURST considered the reduction in the use of gas was owing to the had gas. He thought it strange that more gas was not used considering the increasing population. Councillor BEAMAN also considcred that the decrease in the use of the gas was due to it being so dirty. One of the largest manufacturers was making arrangements for a new illuminant. . _

Councillor SHAW GREEN spoke in support of the sug- gestion if Councillor Monks. Councillor HEPHERD in reply to Councillor Woods said that the average was given by the engineer, and if be knew better than the, engineer, he had better he gas engineer. (Councillor WOODS: That is not an answer to my question). 'rue average was correct as far as he knew. With reference to the suggesi.ion of Councillor Monks, he did not think it was worth while to have fresh books printed with the financial statement.

RIVERS COMMITTEE. Councillor ROBERTS moved the adoption of this Corn- mittee's minutes. He said that the chairman of the Committee (Councillor It. T. Fairclough) with a feeling which did him infinite credit did not propose the adop- tion of the minutes as an important point of law in which Lie was concerned, was pending settlement. He was glad to say the nuisance in the old bed of the river at Willer- spool-road mould soon be abated. It had been decided at the last meeting that the Town Clerk should prepare at once a statement containing the various clauses of the Ship Canal Company's Act, in which th interests of Warrington were involved. That statement the 7 would have in the course of a few days. He might here refer to a notice of motion under the name of Councillor FlOod. They were at present in a delicate position with the Ship Canal, and it would not therefore be to the interest )f the town that a discussion should take place at the present moment. Councillor BOLTON seconded the motion and the min- utes were adopted. .

The minutes of this Committee were proposed by Alderman Hutchinson seconded by Councillor Smethurst.
Councillor BOLTON : What is the reason Councillor Muir has left the Committee ? I thought he was a val- uable member. (Laughter ) The minutes were adapted. WATER COIISIITTEE.

This Committee's minutes appeared in our last issue, and *their adoption was proposed by Alderman FRaNCO3III and seconded by Councillor 11EPHERD. Councillor LONGTON asked how it was that 8141. per cent. of the cost was charged to the Rural Sanitary Authority to extend the new main in Orford. He thought the charge was rather high. Alderman FRANCOMB said that the matter was still in negotiation. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. —TEE RECENT COUNTY

div.head: COUNCIL INQUIRY.
div.p: COUNCIL INQUIRY.

The nainutes of this Committee were proposed by the MAYOR seconded by Alderman FRANCOMR. Councillor BENNETT asked whether it was proposed to take action concerning the remarkable decision of the. Joint Committee which was held on the previous Friday. Be thought that Warrington would suffer a great injus- tice by that decision. The Joint Committee had pro- posed that out of a total number of Guardians of 26, they would only allot nine to Warrington. He did not see why they should put up with this great injustice, seeing that they had five eighths of the area of.the Union and nearly one half of the rateable value. Newton with only a population of 12,000 would have five members. The TOWN CLERN said that he understood th it the Guardians intended to apply to the Local Government Board against the decision of the Joint Committee. It was more a matter for the Union than for the Borough, hut if it was thought advisable, they could make repre- sentations to the Local Government Board upon the matter. Councillor BENNETT said he was glad to hear it. He • would point out that Newton with 12,000 was to have live members, Haydock with 6,000 was to have three, while Warringtan with 53,000 would only have nine members. There were other anomalies equally as great as those pointed om. The Mayon pointed out that the matter would come under the notice of the General Purposes Committee. Councillor ROBERTS said that he supported the spirit of Councillor Bennett's remarks. He thought he knew • sqnnething of the interpretation of the English language and when he saw po3ted on the walls that an inviry ! was rToitr to be held, he took it that an inquiry would be held where everybody would have a right to he pro- sent, and would have a right to speak and submit facts • relative to the inquiry. He never saw anything so utterly in the nature of a sham in his lif, as the inquiry which was held the other day. If instead of sending a Joint Committee, the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils had sent their intentions in writing, it would have been much more respectful to them as a Corpora- tion. The Corporation was treated with scant courtesy ; in fact with positive discourtesy by the Chairm tri, and it seemed perfectly evident from the beginning of the inquiry that the Committee had come with their minds made up,and it did not matter the toss of a button what ever the Corporation suggested. He felt that he was expressing, the sentiments of all those present, and he emplia'icailv protested against the disregard to the inter- est of Warrington shown bv the Chairman. Kan wing a little of the reputation of Mr. V. K. Armitage, he was not surprised that he had been a defeated Liberal candi- date for Parliament on mole than one occasion. (Laugh- ter.) The Mayon agreed with Coancillor Roberts. Mr. SHAW (-Ailed attention on principle to an item of £5 11. ne. for refreshments to the Councillors who went on hoard the Helvetia to see the Queen. He moved an amendment that that sum be not confirmed. He ad- mitted that no was one of the councillors who went to Manchester. The amendment was not seconded, and the minutes of the committee were carried unanimously.

div.head: EXTENSInN OF THE TOWN HALL
div.p: THE EXTENSInN OF THE TOWN HALL

Councillor It T. FAIRCLOGIIII propo.ged a motion of which he had given notice, to the eff•-q;t: that the Council request the Town Hall Sze. Committee not to spend any funds npon enlarging the Town Hall until a c,rnpiet,, plan of the proposed extension he approved. He said that he brought forward the motion h,ca,ue he observed in the year's expenditure of the committee that there was an item of £5OO for increasing the acccommodation of the Town Hall. Seeing that they had already spent £7OO in alterations at the school attendance officesond in preparation for the ,gates, he thought that it would he better to have complete plans. He did not wiF•ll them to put up huildings which would have to come down when further improvements were necessary. •

• Coune,illor HEertErm seconded, and Alderman Su'rr ON supported the motion. Councillor Bouroti• did not. see the necesitv of giving a complete plan of the extension. Plans would bu sub- mitted as alterations were made. The discussion was continued by several inernhers,and the following voted for the motion :-11,1ormen BLick- horst, Sutton, and Ashton ; Councillors R. T. F,ircloneo, Faircloueh. Roberts, Shaw Green, Soilt,nek. son' Shaw, Henherd. Monks, Beaman. Flood, Tinsley, and Woods. No one voted against,. the motion which was therefore carried. WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL. Councillor Fr.oon moved a resolution to the offret that the Rivers and General Purposes C,ommittees he in,. structed to publish a copy of all agreements and cor- respondence entered into by those committees, and the representatives of the Ship Canal having reference to the construction of the Warrington docks, Sze., and also that. a meeting of the Council beheld un,m Juno 20th, to take it into consideration. He said that, lie had been strongly advised to withdraw his motion, and lie Was alwa,vs willing to submit to the opinion of their lee's] advisor. He hid been advised in a friendly manner that it would not he to the het interest of Warrington that the resn- lotion should he passed. They would pardon him if he insisted upon testing the feelings of the Council upon the stibiect. They all knew when the Ship Canal Co., Was likely to become a comin,ercial undertakine, many looked Inward to seeing a turn in the prosperity of W.4r- ringten. 'they were most anxious that everything should be done to promote the progress of the under- taking. He therefore thought that the neeotiations which had passed between the company and the con). mittees should be disclosed. Ile had hen told that there Was nothing to conceal. If that was so why were the tarts not disclosed ? He hoped that the navi- gation of the river won,d be protected, and he wished the impression robe taken away that they were hoed- winked by wiser men than themselves. Councillor BoriEtyrs was proceeding to reply to Conn- cillor Flood, when Cooncillor Flood ro.e to a point of order, and pointed out that as the motion had net been seconded, no one coold speak upon it. Councillor IiOURRTS said that he would second the motion so as to have the opp, rtimity of answering Councillor Flood, although he did not care fel- that method. He ntefe•rn-I1 to do it some other way, because he did not second 'he spirit of the resolution. The TOWN ClFFirc said that Councillor Roberts could ask the permission of the Conned to artdress them. Cooneillor lloncryrs aecordiniely decided not to cee,on,l , the resolutionanfl no other seeonder forthcoming, Coun- cillor Fiord's motion fell to the ground. . Councillor llonuers then obtained kayo to address tl e Council, and said that it Cottecillor Flood or any one else thoneht that the interests of Warrington had teen in any ,nra v j.onardised tiv any art of the Rivers or General poi.pn.se committee, in their negotiations with the Shin Canal, ..'oh itrrreFslong were entirely withctit founds- tion. All the talk about hei.cr hoodwinked shout ar- tsnl brieg made priudicial to IVarrington were

also without foundation. So far as he knew,there was no Judas upon any Committee of the Corporation. There was at present a lawsuit between two members of the Cor- iy,ration and the Ship Canal Company, but their interest in that matter was identical with that of the Corporation. The Corporatiran was looking on and taking care that their interests were not prejudiced by anything done in regard to the Ship Canal Committee. fie believed that instruc- tion had been given to the Town Clerk by the Rivers Committee which would more than meet everything contained in that proposition, and when the Council had before them the whole of the clauses of the Ship Canal Acts in which the interests of Warrington were concerned,then would be the time to ,discuss them. He thought there should not at present be any public dis- cussion for they were in a critical condition, and they were in the position that if the money which was nearly exhausted as far as the Company was concerned was not forthcoming to do that portion of the work which the Company had undertaken to do,they would have to con- sider what they would do in the matter. It was there- fore positively prejudicial to discuss the matter at pre- sent. He would assure the press of Warrington that while they were always glad to see them alive to the interest of the town, the Rivers and General Purposes Committees were not alseep. They were doing all they could that men could do, in the interests of the town, and they were not going to allow those interests to be sacrificed if it was possible to avoid it. The MAYOR thanked Councillor Roberts for his re- marks and said that as long as he was in the chair, he would look after the interests of Warrington. The Council then rose.

div.head: WARRINGTON WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOC IATION: MEETING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOC IATION: MEETING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

On Monday evening a tea party and entertain- ment in connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, was held in the Liberel Club. There was a very large company at the tee; end also at the meeting held subsequently in the Assembly room of the club. The tea, which was an excellent one, was provided by Mr. Mitchell, the manager of the club. The following ladies pre- sided at the tables: Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. W. Roberts, Mrs. Holford, Mrs. Clay, and Mrs. Cavanagh. Among those present at the meeting were Mr. J. Rylands, J.P. (chairman), Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., and Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. Stewart Brown (of Liverpool), Miss B. Dutton, Mrs. l'ierpoint, Councillor and Mrs. H. Roberts, Mr. T. Birchall, J.P., Miss Coubrough, Mrs. and Miss Cavanagh (hon. sec.), Mrs. Holford, Mr. J. H. Fleming, J.P., Mrs. Clay, Mr. I. Hayward, Mr. J. Mounfield, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Garland, Mrs. Wyllie, Mr. and Mrs. W. Roberts, Councillor Plumpton, Misses Pickavance, Mrs. Cook (Latchford), Mrs. G. Carter, Misses Fleming, Mrs. A. H. Rathbone, Mr. and Mrs. G. Browne, Mrs. Perris, and Mrs. Forshaw. Miss CAVANAGH read a letter of apology from Mrs. J. Crosfield who regretted her inability to attend the meet- ing, owing to being away from home. She hoped they would have a gooSmeeting.—Mr. Wm. Pierpoint, J.P., also wrote saying that he was very sorry that an im- portant business engagement would prevent his atten- dance at the meeting. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said that when he came that evening, he thought he would have to begin by saying "ladies" and "not ladies and gentlemen." (Laughter.; Be had expected that the gentlemen were at home taking care of the children. (Laughter.) He had been expecting something of the kind from the signs of the times. However he hoped that the present meeting was really an evidence that the ladies were going to do something. (Hear, hear.) He had been rather concerned at the ideas upon Home Rule. (La.ughter.) With regard to Horne Rule for Ireland, it was quite a different thing, and he was quite prepared to do all he could for that object. Be had been very jealous for a long time of the Primrose League move- ment. He had seen something of it. They did not see much of it in Warrington, but in the village where he lived in the summer in Wales, he saw a great deal of it, and he did not like it. (Hear, hear.) He did not know whether his audience read the proceedings of the Prim- rose League. If they wanted to know what they ought not to say, they had better read them. (Hear, hear and laughter.) There were some very curious habits with the League—habits which were sometimes called bri- bery, and he hoped that the Liberals would never con- descend to imitate them in this respect. (Hear, hear.) They might do a great deal'avithout money in trying to persuade the people to adopt Liberal principles, and it was here that he had great hopes that the women would be able to help on the progress of Liberal principles. (Ap- plause.) They had recently seen how difficult it was for the Liberals to do anything, for they had been met with obstruction of a kind which was most discreditable. (Hear, hear.) It appeared to him that if this could not be prevented, Parliamentary proceedings would become a farce, and the public would be getting disgusted with Parliamentary legislation. (Applause.) He hoped that the Liberals in. Warrington would have better times before long and that the cause would go on and prosper. (Applause.) Mrs. STEWART BROWN, of Liverpoisl, next addressed the meeting. She said that that was not the first oppor- tunity the Warrington Liberal Association had given her of speaking in Warrington. About a year ago sha had the pleasure of opening a sale of work in the town, and she was very much gratified with the kindly recep- tion extended to her. They met that night as a party organization, conbined together to promote Liberal prieeiples, and to help to achieve the success of the Liberal party. She regretted that at present they in Warrington had no Liberal candidate before them, ant she hoped that before many weeks had elapsed, those gentlemen to whom the selection of a candidate was en- trusted, would be able to provide them with one. Shs hoped that they would work for the return of a Liberal at the next election instead of their present Tory mem- ber. She always insisted at the meetings she addre.;sed, that Tory strongholds were simply places where the electors had not yet been sufficiently educated in politi- cal principles, and it was only in the advance of politi- cal education that the Liberals could expect to achieve a triumph. (Applause.) She was well aware that they were beset with exceptional difficulties. They knew well the difficulties she alluded to, and she did not pro- pose to go into detail with them. Those present in the first place, were better calculated to know them ,and it would perhaps be invidious to name them. At the same dine there were great difficulties created by the publicans and public houses in their midst. (Hear. hear.) But there was no reasen to be disceuraged. She proposed that night to endeavour to a.wa ken the womsn to their, responsibititiee to the community atpi well as to their own families and immediete connections. A great number of evils could be coesiderahly remedied if women were to take an active i,:haee in public life. (Applause.) She thought that the purposes (if women would be better served by their joining the Liberal party, than by joining the curious combination of the Censervatiye-Unioeist rart7. (Hear, hear.) She thought that party had no principles at all, except a negative of all the principles advocated and supported by the Leberal party. (Hear, hear.) The Conservative party had ceased to be, in any proper sense- of the word. It might "ne regretted for the oil Conservatives were averse to any change in the pictnreseein institutions of the country. The present Conservative party was not averse to change. They •

I had become similar to the party in France—a party of Opportunists, who were a party of no fixed principles, and supported e.hanges simply to catch votes. They had seen the Conservative party adopt thoroughly Lih- , eral measures, which they had denounced on the plat- , forms in the country. This was the c tse with free sduaa- ' don, and in regard to many other measures. alr.Chatn- berlain, speaking at Bradford, had called attention to certain reforms carried by the last Conservative govern- ment. He did not say who had fought for those reforms in the face of all the opposition of the Tory party. (Applause.) It was very well for the Tories to take credit for passing the reforms. It was the Liberala who had worked for those measures which Mr. Chamber- lain had arrogated to the credit of the Tories. The Liberals had aaitated for the extension of local govern- ment, long before the passing of the County Council Bill, now extended by the Parish Councils Act. They would notice that the reforms of the Tories, had to be per- fected by the subsequent Liberal Government. In the case of free education which was passed by the Tories it was not actually applied until Mr. Acland assumed the reins of the Education Department. (Applause.) She recognised the tremendous loss the Liberal party had sus- tained by the retirement of their beloved leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) They felt that they would never see his like again. (Flear,hear.) But if they had lost him, he had left them a heritage of the noble ex- ample of a man who had raised politics to the highest level they could possibly be raised. (Applause.) He was a wan who never yielded to the influences of corruption or of self interest. She had confidence however that Lord Rosebery would follow in his footsteps. (Ap- plause.) The work of the present Liberal Government 'to carry out its pledges to the electors had been made , very difficult by the obstruction of a deliberate character in the House of Commons,and also in the House of Lords. ' It had not been the fault of the Government that the numerous reforms they had introduced had net passed into law. Those reforms were to the interest of all sec- tions of the community. (Hear, hear.) She was glad that such an advance had been made in the position of the women of the country. This would soon be equal to the men in power, and she urged them to use that 7 ill the right direction. A great danger to the Liberal party at the present time was the danger of it breaking into sections. She was pleased that the Liberal women had kept true to the Liberal party. It might be said that they had no votes and therefore they had no power. But they had great power in influencing the male voters. A great many good Liberals were opposed to ' giving votes to women because they thought that the ' votes would go to the Conservative party. She did not think that would be the case, however, and instanced the case of New Zealand, where the wotnens' franchise ' had been used for the first time, with the result that the Radical party had been returned by an immense ma- jority. It was also found that in municipal elections there was not a large percentage of the women who voted Tory. In conclusion she urged her hearers to work for the Liberal cause in Warrington, and she was sure that their efforts would not be in vain. ( Applause.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said that it gave him great pleasure to be honoured in being requested to move very hearty vote of thanks to Mrs. Stewart Brown for her excellent and able address. (Applause.) It aueured well for the success of the Women's Liberal Association when it could have the services occasionally of ladies with the capacity, and intelligence, and intellectual ability of Mrs. Stewart Brown. (Applause.) There was work for the women in Warrington for a long time to come. (Hear. hear.) They of the sterner sex did not forget that they owed their women friends a debt of gratitude,that they a very short time ago came forward and got them out of debt. (Laughter.) It seemed pro- bable that they would have to look to the women for the resuscitation and revival of the Liberal party in Warrington. (Laughter.) They had seen a great deal of competition for the fair sex on the other side. The Primrose League occasionally offered soma remarkably cheap teas, and it struck him that somebody was be- hind the curtain who had to bear a considerable por- tion of the expense of providing the teas. (Hear, hear.) He as a Liberal " man," felt ashamed for the present position of Liberalism in Warrington. He felt sure that if that association which had had such an excellent meeting that night in spite of such unfavourable weather, would go on and edarate their children in the principles of true Liberalism, the Liberal party in War- rington would soon become much stronger. He was very grateful to Mrs. Brown for her admirable address, and , he had crest pleasure in moving the vote of thanks to her. ( ppl a use. ) _

Mr. T. BrRcirALL seconded the vote of thanks. He said he was sure that Mrs. Brown's address had gone home to every Ane of them. She had shown that the difference between the Tory party and the Liberal party was a very great one. The Liberals had fixed principles and the Pories were simply a party of negetion. They ! (the Liberals) were proud of their principles. He once asked a Tory what were the principles of the Tory party, and this was how he described it. He said that when the coach was going down hill, the brake was a capital . thing to stop it. The Tory party was the brake in this ! country when the coach was going too fast. (Laughter.) That was not a very high position in which to put a party. (Laughter.) They, however, had to complain of the brake being put on when the coach was going up hill instead of letting it go merrily along. (Hear, hear.) ! The vote of thanks was carried unanimously. Mrs. BROWN in her reply said that she did not wish the Women's Liberal Association to follow the example of the Primrose League. She wished them to aim higher than cheap teas and dances and that sort of thing. Mrs. Brown at this point had to leave the meeting, and a musical entertainment was held. An enjoyable programme was gone through, in which Miss Cavanagh and Miss Cniihrouah contributed songs with their usual ability. Miss Bessie Dutton also gave a recital,for which she received well merited applause. The humorous part of the evening was taken by Mr. Forster, who was en- cored for the comic song, "Macnamara's Band," and Mr. . Whittle whose piece was one of Albert Chevallier's coster son entitled "Ytiss," which he gave with much gusto. lie was accompanied on the piano liay Mr. Finch. The accompanist in the other musical items was Mr. Caldwell.

During an interval Miss fiEsstu DUTTON addressed the meetint,P. She expressed her pleasure at the magnificent soreelt of Mrs. Stewart Brown. They wanted to induce al th,se present to join the Women's Liberal Associa- tion. There were some present who did not belong to it. Some women thought that joining the association meant' having to undertake canvassing work, and other work they had a repugnance to, hut all that was wanted was their occasional presence and the small subscription of threepence. There were,therefore,no obstacles to any- body. Then, again, women cught to have votes, and she was sure that if that was so, a great advance would be made in temperance legislation. She therefore hoped that Women's franchise would soon come to pass. In conclusion, she asked that everyone who wished to join would give in their namPs to Miss Cavanagh, who was the secretary, and would always be glad to receive names.

At the conclimi•An or the meetinv. Mr. C. J. Houtxs pr.posed a vote of thank, to the Chairman for presiding over the meeting that night. He said that at his some- what advanced age Mr. Rylands put to shame some ether mernhersof the association in coming out that inclement eveninu.. (Hear, hear.) He would also take that oppor- tunity of announcing that on Tuesday next, the sewing meetings would be commenced, and he as treasurer would he pleased if the women would come down as niinwrotislv as possible. The result of the sale of work last year had been very welcome and hut for it, he was afraid that the association would have had an adverse

balance. He would like to include in the vote of thanks, Mr. Caldwell, who had accompanied during the musical portion of the evening. They were very much indebted to him for his presence. Mr. J. H. FLEMING seconded the vote of thanks. He said that he never expected to see Mr. Hylands there on such an inclement night.. He hoped that Mr. Hylands would long live to come -amongst them. (Hear, hear.) He had been a staunch Radical all his life. He (Mr. Fleming) was glad to see so many in that room, as he had been beginning to fear that they were going steadily backwards. He hoped, however, that the ladies would arise in their wrath—(laughter) —and endeavour to bring about a different state of things. The motion was carried with acclamation, and Mr. RTLANDS in reply complimented them noon the enter- tainment they had had that night. Mr. Fleming had alluded to the fact of his having a good deal to do with politics during his long life. He could hot help thinking about it when Mrs. Stewart Brown was speaking. Ever since he could remember he had been constantly fighting against privilege and Toryism. He remembered he days of the Corn Laws agitation, and remembered per- fectly well Cobden and Bright coming to Warrington and speaking at a meeting at the Lion Hotel. He could remember John Bright in speaking of an aristocrat say- ing that he would like to switch him, to which Cobden replied " Why John, if you had not been a Quaker, you would have been a prize-fighter." (Laughter.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF A BOY,
div.p: THE NARROW ESCAPE OF A BOY,

Our issue of last week described the extraordinary cure of a boy named Coupe. On inquiry, the father,Mr- John Coupe, of 7, Holly-st., Burnley, a well-educated and respected citizen, states that the present condition of the lad ia very satisfactory indeed. "We consider him " writes Mr. Coupe—referring to the cure of the dying boy by a safe and extraordinarily effective medi- cine, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale Peopl,.—" in a better state of health than ever before in his life. He used to have rheumatic pains, and his legs were para- lysed, but from first t iking, Dr. Williams Pink Pills there was a steady improvement. He took them for some months, and has now no rheumatics, and is no longer paralys3d, but has good use of his legs, eats well, sleeps well, and is getting both bigger and stronger." Suffer- ers whom ordinary medicine fails to cure, or who need a nerve tonic and blood foll, shluld obtain from their chemists the same valuable medicine.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

_ . In the House of Commons on Monday evening the House again went into C-unmittee on the Budget 8111. Commander BETHELL moved an amendment to provide that the estate duty should be levied under the same c•cnditions and at the same rates as the existing probate and estate duties. In the coorse of the discussion Sir W. HARCOURT said the principle of graduation was the corner-stone of the Budget, and upon that principle the Budget would stand to fall. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he should vote with the Government. On a division there voted :—For the amendment, 105 ; against 290. Clause 1 was then agreed to nem con.

TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Mr. Maclure moved that the House should at it rising ad- journ over Derby day. Mr. Chaplin seconded the motion. Sir W. FIARCOURT said the Government had come to the conclusion that the House of Commons had no right to appropriate the time of the House to any other purpose than that for which it was given last week. The motion was defeated by 248 to RD. Tile House then went into Committee again on the Budget Bill. At midnight pro- gress was reported. 'WEDNESDAY.

The House of Commons again went into Committee on the Budget Bill on Wednesday. On clause 2 Sir R. Temple moved an amendment to omit a reference to v-luntary settlements described by Mr. Balfour as being intended to bring under duty money passing by mar- riage settlements. Sir W.Hanconar said the great bulk of the property of the country passed by will. It was only the wealthier classes who :lad settlements,and there was no reason why they should not pay mi them. The amendment was negatived. A good deal of discussion arose on an amendment moved by Mr. Courtney to exempt joint annuities not exceeding £lOO. Sir W. HARCOURT said he should be prepared to exempt exist- ing reversions purchased for full value,and Mr. COURT- NEY said he would not press the atnend meat, which was by leave withdrawn. Other amendments were negatived or withdrawn,and one moved by Mr. Byrne was defeated by 192 to 145. Mr. H. flobhouse moved an amendment to provide that the estate duty should not be payable on any property passing from a wife to a husband or a hus- band to a wife, and it waq supported by Mr. Betrotm. who said the bill struck a, blow at the whole idea cf community of interest assumed in the rest of our legis- lation to exist between husband and wife. Sir W. HAR- coma said that on property under £25,000 the bill made no increase, and that this amendment would diminish the revenue. The amendment was under discussion when the hour for adjournment of the debate arrived. ! The Prevention of Cruelty to Children Bill was read a third time and passed. A bill to empower boards of guardians to grant relief to persons in receipt of allowances from friendly socie- ties was also read a third time.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

On Tuesday evening the monthly meet in of the above hoard was held in the Thwn Hall, Runcorn, under the presidency of Mr. James Pritchard. The remaining gentlemen present were the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Dr. 111cDougall, Messrs. T. Handley, S. Taylor, E. unison, G. Moss, clerk.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

This Committee held meetings on May Bth and 29th, and the minutes of the proceedings show that 66 parents had been summoned out of which 54 appeared. It was decided to take proceedings against 16 parents. The visitors reported that the scholars en the hooks during the month ending May 25th numbered 3,478 against 3,700 twelve months previous: decrease 222 ; averaue attendance 2,897 compared with 3,089 last year: de- crease, 192; percentage, 83.3 being the same as last year. The Committee recommended that three children be sent to the School for Blind in Hardman-street, Liverpool, the Board to pay for the maintenance of each child £2l per annum, which sum would include clothing. Alsn that a boy be sent to St. John's Institution tor Deaf and Dumb, Boston Spa, York,hiro ; the Board to pay £l6 per annum for his maintenance and clothing.— Dr. McDougall asked whether it had been accertaineci how much the parents of each of these children could contribute towards their maintenance.—A lengthy dis- cussion followed during which it was stated that rertain enquiries had been made bearing upon that point and others would necossarilv follow in order that the rate- payers might not be called upon to contribute an undue amount.—Eventually Mr. Taylor, as a member mf the Committee, moved the adoption of the minutes which was seconded by Canon Wood and carried.

SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. The Clerk read the minutes of this committee aryl also the following recommendations :—The. Miss Edith McLean, monitor of the Greenwa:--rn,d Girls School, he appointed pupil teacher, at a salary a",cording to the Board's scale. That Miss Annie Dyer he appointed pupil teacher at the Mill Brow Infants School at a salary according to the Board's scale. Both appoint- ments are contingent upon the teachers passing the requisite examinations. Further that the tender of Mr. T. J. Kirkham for alterations at the Mill Brow school be accepted.—Mr. Handley proposed the confirmation of the minutes. Dr. McDougall seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: WEST,EYAN DAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE WEST,EYAN DAY SCHOOLS.

The Chairman announced that the Managers of the Brunswick and Granville-street Wesleyan Das- Schools had decided to continue the school; for another twelve months. This arrangement would prove advantageous to the parents of the children who attended the schools and also the Board who were at present negotiating with the managers regarding the question and terms of transfer.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF A CARETAKER.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF A CARETAKER.

The Clerk stated that he had received a letter from Mr. Berry resigning his post of caretaker of the Green- way-road hoard Schools.—The resignation was accepted. and arrangements have been made for securing a success Jr.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNIt 9, 1894

TEE statement which Sir Jomyr Tile Canal. HARWOOD made at the Manchester City Council on Wednesday reveals Leerious state of things in regard to the finances the Ship Canal Company. To the shareholders t It -e e°/npany and to the ratepayers of Manches- r BuPplieB much food for anxious reflection. litt Will be remembered that in 1801 the Manches- ,..er Corporation decided to provide the additional lunds that were then found necessary to complete 'the Canal. The Company itself had, so to speak, reached the end of its financial tether. Its bor- eh:ing Powers were exhausted, and there was no tCnce of its raising or obtaining new capital in 4.:e °Pen market. An appeal was, therefore,made o the Manchester Corporation to raise a loan on the security of the city rates, and this appeal was by with. Judging from the statement made •Y Sir jelni HARWOOD this week, the City Coun. , seeing to have made its new andrisky departure a very unbusinesslike way. The Canal Company _B4 desperately in need of more cash,but as is the 7113' With borrowers, it represented its position is .1.!le most favourable light. It was for the Corpora- • m°n, in its capacity as lender, to make strict in- . ' vairies WI to the extent of the liabilities it was .It,hc'ut to undertake. This it did not do; hence tie disappointing chapter of events which Sir JOHN kt"MOOD commented upon. In January,of 1891, Lord EftERTON, the Chairman of the Canal Corn- in asking for the .assistance of the Corpora- lon, estimated the additional sum necessary to • -11ei°tilrplete the Canal to be £ 1,700,000. A tle superficial inquiry by the Manchester *.ater engineer quickly brought this sum up to - 2,313,173, and in the end the Corporation ob- tained Parliamentary power to lend £3,000,000. IS large amount was rapidly expended, and another £2,000,000 had to be raised on the same tiecuritY• The £2,000,000 appears to be vanishing ‘4,llicklY, and still the end is not yet in sight. As we have said it Was clearly the policy and the duty of the Manchester Corporation to make very search- 42itlidee before it advanced it; iniiiionsi and

therefore the complaints now made by Sir JOHN HARIVOOD of having been misled come rather late in the day. In some instances the estimates sub- mitted to the Corporation were so evidently be- low the mark that their inadequacy should not have been overlooked. Take,for instance,the sum of -290,500 for "dock equipment, sheds, &c." A little consideration might have shown that £90,500 was not likely te provide the "dock equipments, &c." of so largo an undertaking as the Ship Canal, As a matter of fact, it has now been found that the sum under this heading should have been , £447,29d.” Then, again, it was estimated that £5,500 would cover the extensive responsibilities of the Canal Company with regard to their inter- ference with Wigg's chemical works at Runcorn. In reality, the Company have had to pay "no less a sum than £BO,OOO in fulfilling the requirements of the firm under the Act." The same differences between estimates and actual expenditure are ob- servable to a certain extent with respect to the , Partington coal tips, and the diversion of the river at Arpley Meadows, Warrington. The coal tips were estimated to cost £lO,OOO ; they have al- ready cost £46,000, and will probably requiro another £lO,OOO. The Arpley diversion, with the dredging necessary in connection with it, was to be accomplished at an outlay of £2,500; but already £12,000 has been spent and £lO,OOO more is required. With estimates expanding at this rate, it is not surprising that the Corporation directors have been alarmed, and that Sir JOHN HARwoon, the chief of them, expresses a desire to leave the work in other hands. As to the position that the Manchester Corporation is likely to find itself in, it is, perhaps, • premature to speak. Sir JOHN HARWOOD'S forecast is not re-assuring. He says he has warned the Consultative Committee that if something drastic be not done, the Cor- poration will in 1896 have to find money for the interest on debentures, and that will mean a rate of one shilling and eightpence in the pound. In addition to this, there are" the numerous and onerous obligations entered into by the Canal Company under their van i ous Acts of Parliament." it is singular that SirJoHNHAnwoon should now say that he and the other Corporation directors have been ignorant of these obligations until recently, obligations which, as he himself says, "will largely drain the resources even of the Manchester Cor- poration." The Acts in which these obligations are set forth have, all along, been easily accessible, and it does, therefore, seem a reflection upon the Corporation that it s hould pledge itself to the extent of £5,000,000 before inquiring into the liabilities it was incurring.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday morning, before Mr. F. J. Norman, James Robinson was lined ss. and costs or in default of payment seven days'imprison- ment, for having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge- street on the morning of the 4th inst.—P.C. Gregory proved the charge. COLLIE/I'N BLACK BLENDED TEA, 20. per quarter lb.—Advt. THEFT or COAL AT WIDNES.—SENTENCE AT THE SESSIONS. At the Liverpool County Intermediate Sessions held on Tuesday, Mary Jane Doyle, of Warrington-road, Widnes, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment for having stolen 20Ibs. of coal, at Widnes, on the 51st May, the property of the United Alkali Co. Limited. . Success or Mn. J. CLoodia, FORMERLY or RuNcoeN. We are ple,ased to state that Mr. J. Clough, late organ- ist at the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcor n,has been successful in his application for the positiGn of organist and choirmaster at Edge Hill Congregational Church, Liverpool. Mr. Clough was a much respected gentleman, both on account of his kindly disposition and undoubted musical skill, and his friends in Run- corn will be pleased to hear of his success. GOLLIER'S sell the best quality goods at lowest possible prices.—Advt. FLOWER SERVICE AT THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CuerEL, RUNCORN.

Special flower services were conducted on Sunday morning, afternoon, and evening at this chapel, when eloquent sermons were delivered by Mr. J. Spruce, of Preston Brook, and the Rev. James Hanby, of Halton. The congregations at each service was large, and the re- marki of the gentlemen mentioned were fully appre- ciated. In the evening Mr. H. Woodward rendered the solo "Nothing but leaves," in a most commendable manner. The floral decorations, which were exeedingly tasteful, had been carried out by members of the Chris- tian Endeavour Society. Mr. W. Glittens, jun.,presided at the organ with ability. The collections realised £5 I'.6d. ,a considerable increase on last year. This amount will be devoted to the Circuit fund. COLLIER'S FRESH IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, 10d. per lb is eceellent.— Advt.
Two RECENT RESIDENTS OF RUNCORN KILLED AT DOTER.

A shocicing accident occurred on the 30th May at the Dover Harbour extension works and resulted in the death af two men named Thomas Manktn and Samuel Rowley, both of whom were well-known in Runcorn through being engaged on the local section of the Manchester Ship Canal during its construction. From particulars to hand it appears that the men were employed by Messrs. Jackson and Co., contractors for the harbour works at Dover. They were helping to raise a girder which, when loosened by the men, swung inwards and crushed them. Upon the girder re-bounding both men felloverboard and when picked up Rowley was dead. Mankin died during his removal to the hospital. An inquiry was made on the following day into the circumstances by the Coroner and a jury, who, after a lengthy sitting returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death," and added. a rider to the effect that the proper authorities be urged to take every i possible precaution to prevent the recurrence of similar accidents. The funeral of the two men took place on Friday afternoon when about 80 of their fellow-workmen joined the procession of mourners SUNDAY SCIPOOL ANNIVERSARIES AT WIDNES. The anniversary services in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School were held cn Sun- day and Monday. Sermons were preached, on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev. W. E. Lead. In the afternoon a service of song entitled "Golden deeds" was given by the scholars, Mr. A. E. Calvert presiding. The service was given in an admirable manner, the vari- ous recitations, solos, duets, choruses, he., being ren- dered in excellent style. On Manday evening a public tea party was held and afterwards a miscellaneous pro- gramme was gone through. The Vicar of Widnes (the Rev. W. Hodgson, M.A.) presided. A. most enjoyable programme of music was rendered by the following : Misses Hosker, and 'Guise, and Messrs . H. Williams, Stringer, Johnson, T. A. Brady, A. Shingler, and J. Thompson. The collection on Sunday amounted to £4B oq.3d.—The anniversary in connection with the Halebank Wesleyan Sunday School was celebrated on Sunday. Special sermons were preached in the morning and even- ing by the Rev. John Gunnell of Penketh. At night there was a crowded attendance. Special hytnns were sung by the scholars and choir. Collections were taken at both services in aid of the Sunday Schoolfunds, and amounted to £lO. COLLIER'S sell everything for the smallest possible prott.— Advt.
94T11 ANNIVERSARY OF THE BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL,
RuNconN.

Arrangements are now complete for celebrating the 94th anniversary of the Brunswick Sunday School, Run- corn. On Sunday the 17th inst., the pulpit at St. Paul's Church, will be occupied morning and evening by the Rev. W. L. Watkinson, of London, who is editor of the "Methodist Magazine." As a popular preacher Mr. Watkinson is held in high repute, and his visit is antici- pated with the keenest pleasure. We feel sure that Runcornians will not fail to embrace so favourable an opportunity of hearing so distinguished a divine. On the following Monday night a public meeting will be held, when Mr. Watkinsen will speak at length on Sun- day School work. The interest in this meeting will be considerably enhanced by the fact that Mr. John Simp- son will deal with the history and objects of the institu- i tion at Runcorn. His connection with the school,covers a period vergimr on 60 years, and his retniniscenses therefore will afford much pleasure to the general pub- lic ; while for old and young Brunswiekites they must possess a very peculiar charm, The chair will be occu- pied by Mr, J.
