div.head: SUCCESS OE A VVIDNES CYCLIST.
div.p: SUCCESS OE A VVIDNES CYCLIST.

! At Leigll Amateur Athletic sports on Saturda,y, Win. ' Jackson, ~f I,vidnas, won the mile bicycle race, after a dead heat by half a wheel. WEST BANK MISSION BALL, WIDNES. On Saturday evening a service of sang entitled" The Little Pilgrim " was given by the members of the Band of Hope in connection with the above mission and a few friends. The service of song was given in excellent style and was greatly enjoyed. An admirable miscel- laneous programme followed. The Rev. J. Adams pre- sided. The object of the entertainment was to raise funds for a treat to the children.

WIDNES SOAP WORKS. This business, which has for a great length of time been known under the name of Wm. Gosage and Sons, has been converted into a limited liability company.and will in future be known as William Gossage and Sons, Limited. As the change has been made for family rea- sons no shares will be offered to the public.all being held by the present partners, their sons, and the managers. COLLIER'S IS. BUTTER is the gem in the market.—Advt. EXCULSION OF RUNCORN CYCLISTS TO CHESTER.

On Wednesday afternoon the midweek riders of the Runcorn Cycling Club mustered in stong force in Dover- shire square and at 2 15 prompt started on an intended excursion to Farndon. I hey took the route by way of Frodsham and Helsby, but on arriving at Chester the sky was so overcast with threatening clouds that the projected spin had to be abandoned. As it was only four o'clock the members put put their machines into safe keeping, and enjoyed a sail down the Dee almost as far as Farndon. They returned to Chester, and partook of an excellent tea at the Liver Hotel. After this meal was over an hour or more was spent in various kinds of amusement, when the party remounted their iron steeds and steered towards the " good old town" again, which they reached after a pleasant run.

ANOTHCR WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES. On Thursday at the Widnes Petty Ses-ions 1-aforo Messrs. F. Stapleton Bretherton and W. 14,13 Pilkington, Bridget Feeney. 11, Moss-street, was brought up on re- mand charged with unlawfully wound* Patrick Murphy, with intent to do him grevious bodily harm,on Sunday afternoon, by striking him on the head with a lieCe of earthenware pipe. It appears that whilst prosecutor was eating his dinner, the prisoner came in- to his house by the back door and hit him on the head with a piece of drain pipe. He fell to the floor, and she kicked him on the head until he became insensible. Dr. O'Keefe dressed the wounds, and he reported that their was an incised wound 2i inches in length and penetrat- ing to the bone. The prosecutor now wished the charge withdrawn, and this was allowed on prLoner piyiug costs and doctor's fee.

div.head: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.

The following letter signed by Mrs. Silcox, as presi- dent and Miss Calver; and Miss Robinson, as secreta% ie , of the Widnes Branch of the above association, tias been forwardid to Mr. Gilliatt at the House of Corn. mons :—Sir.—We are directed by the committee of the Widnes Bratr.th of the British Women's Temperance Association to request that, in the consideration ot the Registration Bill now before Parliament, you will give your vote and influence in favour of any instruction or amendment thereto, whereby women shall be entitled to the Parliamentary Franchise on the same terms as men and thereby remove the injustice of denying the rights of citizenship to many who are subject to all its reTonsibilities in violation of the fundamental maxim of the constitution that representation shall acco m2any taxation.

div.head: JUVENILE THIEF AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A JUVENILE THIEF AT RUNCORN.

' At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday morning before Dr. Steele and Mr. F. J. Norman a small boy named Albert Walker eleven years of age was charged with stealing a black worsted vest,value ss. 61 the pro- perty of Messrs. Unsworth Bros. ,clothiers, Iligh-street,on the 2nd inst.—Frederick Kersley, assistant at Messrs. Unsworth's shop, spoke to hanging the vest, among other articles of wearing apparel, outside the shop on Saturday morning. When taking the things in at night he missed the vest.—John Arthur Smith engaged at the pawnshop of his father in Alcock-street, deposed to re- ceiving the vest (produced) from the boy on Saturday night at about 10 o'clock. He gave his MUM, as John Walker and as he had been in the habit of visitino. the shop witness did not ask him any questions but allowed him is. 6d. upon the garment.—P S. Lea testified to apprehending the boy on Saturday night who upon being charged admitted the theft saving that he had given is. to his mother and had spent 6d. himself. When witness spoke to the mother about the affair she replied that her son had told her that he had picked the money up from the ground at the Market place.—Elaving confessed that lie had committed the theft the boy was ordered to a reformatory school for five years. COLLIER'S is the best money can buy.—Advt. SUPPOSED SUICIDE etT WIDNES.—TIE INQUEST.

On Sunday afternoon a boy named Thomas Mac- Dermott was walking on the shore of the river Mersey Rear Widnes Mash when he saw something lying on ti • foreshore. He found that it was the ly.dy of a man. Information was given to lospector Strickland and Sergeant Radcliffe, who had the body conveyed to the Commercial Hotel, wh ere it was identified as that of William Jackson, a coloured man, aged 65 years, of 42, Oxford-street, Widnes. It appears that up to July 1893, deceased was employed as a labourer by the Widnes Local Board and Corporation. He had, since that time, worked for about six months, as a labourer at Messrs. Ga6kell Deacon and CO.'B works, but he was eischarged about eleven weeks ago. He has, since then, been in a very depressed state of mind and has told his wife on several occasions, when going out in search of work, that she might never see him again. On Tnursday the 24th May, on his leaving home to go to Gaskell Deacon's works in search of work, he said to his wife "Good-bye, you may never see me again." He was not again seen alive after that date.—On Wed- nesday afternoon Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy county coroner, held an inquest at the Widnes Police Court, touching the death. After hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." They suggested that a mortuary should be provided in the borough.

ST. LUKE'S CONGREGATIONAL SABBATH SCHOOL, RUNCORN. By reference to our advertising columns it will be seen that the anniversary services in connection with the above school will he held on Sunday in the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn. In the morning and evening the pulpit will be occupied by- Mr. A. Bathgate, of Aigburth, who has won a well-deserved reputation as a preacher. In the afternoon Mr. Phillip France, of Malpas, will address both parents and scholars at the St. Luke's Chapel, Pennington-row, which is in reality the present institution of the Bethesda Church, having been built more than a score of years before the latter. An incalculable amount of good work is being done in the district by the school, and we are sure that all Christian persons will subscribe in as liberal a manner as their means will allow them. The funds are not only required to carry on the spiritual education of the chil- dren, but also to give them free treats at different periods of the year, towards which the scholars look for- ward with joyful anticipation. The membership is at ; present 180, the average attendance 150; and the annual expenditure is between £2O and £3O. The amount seems very smalrindeed when it is considered that the lives of so many children are made happy and profitable thereby. Special hymns and anthems will be sung by the choir and school children and it is hoped that the congrega- tions will be large and the donations generous. SAD bIATI OF A RUNCORNIAN IN CEYLON.

An extensive feeling of regret has been created in Runcorn by the news that Mr. Wm. Humphrey Richards of Runcorn, died on Friday,the Ist inst.,from sunstroke at Ceylon. Mr. Richards, who was 40 years of age,waa well known in Runcorn and district,having been engaged on the Manchester Ship Canal at Weston Marsh Lock wkere he held a responsible position for six years. Lie left Beacon Rill, Weston Point, accompanied by his family when the section was completed, and took up his residence in York-st., Runcorn. On Good Friday last having been appointed general foreman of the bar- bout extension works at Ceylon, by the Gorernment,he I set sail for that island, and arrived there in less than al month. Information was received by the family on &it- urday afternoon last, that he was setiously ill with sun- stroke. This news gave rise to considerable anxiety, but at the same time hopes were entertained that the nature of his illness was not dangerous. Mrs. Richards wishing to know further particulars of her husband's condition communicated with the authorities in Ceylon by telegraph, and on Monday she received She distress- ing rents, that her husband had passed away on Friday. The delay in making the truth known was pi obably pur- posely caused in order that the family might be a little more prepared to hear the worst. The deceased was a member of the Ellesmere Lodge (750) of Freemasons, and leaves a widow two daughters and two sons to mourn his loss.

div.head: RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.

Mr. H. McLeod presided over the annual meeting of the members of the above club which was held on Tues- day evening. There was a large attendance of members. Mr. H. E. Annett, secretary, stated that the season closed on Saturday, April 28th, in a victory of 7 goals to 1 against Weaverharn St. Mary's Ist on the home ground. The season on the ‘N hole had been fairly creditable to the club. 23 matches had been played of which 10 were won, 10 lost and 3 drawn. The scoring also had been fairly even, 55 for and 65 against. The following players were responsible for most of the scoring :.—J. Jones 13. W. Peacock 12, F. Abel 7, J. Lenton 6, J. Hattipson 5, E. Douglas 5. Efforts were being made to secure a better and more accessible field for the next season, and also to make the club a still greater success. Mr. B. Timmins, treasurer, presented the balance sheet for the past season,which showed that the receipts were £l5 9. 9d. ; and the expend:ture £l6 Os. 8. ; thus leaving a balance against the club of 193. 11d.—The reports were adopted on the motion of Mr. W. Carter, seconded by Mr J. Hampson. Messrs. 11. E. Annett and H. Timmins having resigned their posts, Messrs. W. E. Haugh and H. McLeod were appointed to fill the vacan- cies respectively. Messrs. J. Hampson and W. Peac,ck were respectively elected captain and sub-captain of the Ist team. The remaining elections were le ft over for the next meeting which will take place in July. It was decided that the club (Motu fa; next sellaoll be Cambridge

div.p: ANOTHER CASE OF RABIES AT WIDNES. On Saturday information was given to the police that a dog was behaving in a Strange manner near Appleton Quarry.—Superintendent Keighley, Inspector Strickland and P. S. Bennett went in search of it and found it in the yard of the Widnes Foundry,where the animal was shot by P.S.Bennett. Mr. Shawcross, veterinary 'inspector to the Windes Corporation, made a post mortem examination, and certified that the dog had suffered from rabies, This is the second case in the borough within a few days.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT THE GYMNASIUM.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT THE GYMNASIUM.

The season at the Gymnasium was concluded on Monday evening in a pleasant manner, the mem- bers and their friends indulging in a very enjoyable soiree. A pleasing incident occurred during the evening, namely, the presentation to Mr. and Mrs. Kinsley,the conductor and his wife, of suitable pre- sents, as a recognition of their valuable services to the institution during the season. The presents had been subscribed for by the members of the various classes.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS EXCURSION.
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS EXCURSION.

The members of the Warrington Mud of Guar- dians and the officials of the Union, making alto- gether a party of GO, had their annual picnic on Tuesday, when they travelled in 'buses, supplied by Messrs. Maginn Bros., to Knutsford, and Alderley Edge. The enjoyment of the party, however, was somewhat marred by the inclement state of Oil weather. A substantial lunch was partaken of at Hotel, Knutsford, and in the even- ing,the " dinnerß e(1 C owwa supplied at Alderley Edge. The party arrived home at a rather late hour in the evening, the journey being made in a constant downpour of rain. THE POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS AT EARLESTOWN.

In accordance with the resolution passed at the meeting of Commissioners on Monday, in regard to the postal questions at Earlestown, a deputation consisting of Messrs. J. W. Emmett, J. Smith, T. Ormand and R. Brierley, waited upon Mr. J. D. Rich, the post-master at Liverpool, on Thursday. Mr. Rich received the deputation, who laid before him all the matters which at present are agitating the people of Earlestown in relation to the postal arrangements. All the points were fully gone into. and Mr. Rich promised to give the question his full- est consideration. Ile also undertook to keep the .Earlestown post office open for the transaction of postal business, such as the sale of stamps, &sc., until 9 o'clock in the evening. A deputation of ratepayers consisting of Dr. Mouncey, Messrs. T. Molyneux, S. Harvey, and H. Siddeley also had an audience of Mr. Rich at the same time. WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION : THE VACANCY ON THE COUNTY COUNCIL.

_ A special meeting or the council of the Warring- ton Conservative Asiociatien was held on Monday evening, in Vie Assembly Room at the Conservative Club. Mr. John White, J.P., wasin the chair, and amongst those present were Alderman Sutton (hon. secretary), Aldertnvn Francomb (depury-mavor), Alderman Asliton,Ahlerman Wright and Councillors Baird, Smethurst, Skelton, Greening, Shaw, Hill, Muir. On the motion of Alderman Sutton, Mr. John White was re-elected chairman of the associa- tion. Alderman Francomb was re-elected vice- chairman, and beveral committees were appointed. The next business was the selection of a candidate as successor to Mr. Lewis Voisey, who has resigned his position as a County Councillor for Lancashire for N 0.3 ward for the borough, which is co-exten- sive with the Howley, St. Austin's, and Latchford wards.—The Chairman explained that Mr. Voisev had resigned owing to ill-health and pressure of business engagements. His term of office would have expired in March next. The arrangement had been that the Liberals should nominate for one of the three wards, the Liberal Unionists for another ward, and the Conservatives for the third ward. The Conservntives nominated for No. 3 ward, but that did not mean that no one else could nominate. The General Purposes Committee of the association had had the matter under their consideration; and, without wishing to dictate to the meeting in any way, they had decided to recommend three names, out of which a selection would have to be made that evening. They were Alderman Francomb, Alderman Sutton, and Mr. John Fairclough. On the last occasion Mr. Fairclouqh was approached he declined to accept office. Upon the proposition of Councillor Muir,Alderman Francomb was selected as a candidate for the vacancy.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS;
SIONE RS.

The monthly meeting of the Board took place on ' Thursday morning at the Town Hall, Mr. S. Taylor presiding. The other gentlemen present were Dr. B. Mangan, Messrs. P.Speaktnan,J.P., C.C., W.Hand- ley,J. Pritchard, D. Bisbrown,E. iwison, H Abel,W. Collier, W. Leach, H. J. GricP' J. Meadowcroft, J. Dobson, and W. Fisher; F. A. bake,. law clerk; E. Marshall, secretary ; and NI. Barker, surveyor. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. McDougall's report for the month showed that 20 deaths had been registered of which one was the object of a coroner's inquiry. These deaths made an average death rate for the twelve months of twelve per thousand of the estimated population. Exclusive of the inquest. , case the rate would be 10.4. (Hear, hear.) The num- ber of deaths in the corresponding period of last yeat was 36.—Mr. Imison remarked that the Board migh congratulate Dr. McDougall upon his very satisfactory report and also his apparently improved health cmse- quent upon his recent holidays. He (Mr. Itnison) was very pleased to see that Mr. McDougall had returned in such good form. (Hear, hear.) The report was adopt- ed. .

div.head: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Death has removed from our midst another gen- tleman whose name was familiar to all of us, not only on account of his frequent appearance on our magisterial bench and at many of the political meet- ings in the town, but also because of his generosity towards those needilig assistance. The late Mr. Reynolds was a very useful public servant, and had gained the respect and esteem of a wide circle of friends both in Lancashire and Cheshire. There is not the least doubt that his loss will be keenly felt by a large number of persons, more especially by the poor, who have, so often experienced his muni- ficence and consideration wheu.suffering any severe reverse of fortune.

A most important and pertinent query was put by Mr..lmison at a meeting of the school board on Tuesday evening. It had reference to the letting of the Board's contracts for structural alterations and repairs to the different Echools. He stated that there was an idea in the minds of a large propor- tion' of the business men in the town that the whole of this kind of work was done by one firm only, instead of its being distributed amongst all of them or at leas:, those of them who were ratepayers, and who would execute the work at a reasonable figure. He found no fault whatever with the manner in which the work was done,but simply wished to state that should there be any truth in the idea that the whole .of the work was being done by one indi- vidual,a slight alteration ought to be made in future, so that everyone might have a chance of doing some thing, especially in the face of the present scarcity of work. It was answered that tke contract of the work at Mill Brow School was the only one of that description which the Board had ever made, and that in'this case the amount was too small to ren- der it necessary to apply for tenders. This explana- tion does not, however, make the least alteration in the case,-and it is to he hoped thab if such a monopoly exists the Board will not allow it to con- tinue.

The monthly report presented by Dr. McDougall, as Medical Officer of Health, to the Runcorn Com- missioners•at their monthly meeting on Thursnay, has given the most lively satisfaction. The health °Me town must be exceptionally good compared with what it was twelve months ago as is plainly shown by the death-rate. In the past month there has been twenty deaths, one of which was the sub- ject of a coroner's inquiry, against 36 in the cor- responding period of last year. On the face of it this is a very satisfactory condition of things. Let us hope that the health of the community will still continue to improve, or at least to remain as it is, for mane years to come.

When are we going to have a reply from the Manchester Ship Canal Company, regarding the provision of a graving dock or their alternative scheme? We have waited very patiently for some weeks now, but it looks as though we shall have to exercise our patience a little more before we find ourselves in a position to rest satisfied. The sub- ject was one of discussion at the Commissioners meeting on Thursday, being introduced by the chairman announcing that a deputation of painters shipwrights, and boiler makers were anxious to !wait upon him with regard to the matter. The majority of the memherS were agreed that it was a ,1 question of the first importance, affecting the interests of the townspeople to a great extent, and it was decided that a committee of the whole Board should hear the arguments advanced by the depu- tation in reference to the subject.

Tne question of providing public baths for the town is also commanding a fair amount of atten- tion. At the same meeting it was stated by. Mr. Handley that the Committee in charge of the matter had not been idle but had held one meeting and they intended to hold another shortly. Ile expected that they would gather a great deal more at the next meeting and would be in a position to report something of a definite nature to the July assembly of members.

div.head: BIEFHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.
div.p: BIEFHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

' This committee recommended that the application of Mr. T. Bradshaw for leave to put out a bay window to house in Cawley-street be granted—That the tender of Mr. John Sefton for the private street works to be done in Brackley-street, Suffold-street, Ca wdor-street, Port- land-street, Bentinck-street and Leinster-street be accepted.—That the sum of £2 be paid towards the alteration of convenience at the " Lion Hotel," Green- way-road, on condition that it be lined with white glazed bricks to the satisfaction of the surveyor and subject to the money being returned in the event of its being closed to the public at au F thne.—That the following plans be , approved :—Mrs. Kirkham, erection of house near the j canal hank to the westward of Highfield Tannery ; Mr. A. B. Norman, alterations to" Linden Lodge " ; and Mr. • G. White, addition of bathroom to house in Heath-road. —The Chairman moved the adoption of the minutes, subject to an alteration being made in the one having reference to the Lion Hotel. Some misunderstand- ing had occurred and it now appeared that the Board's proportion • of . the cost was £5 instead of £2.—Mr. Bisbrown seconded.—Mr. G.,ace enquired from the Chairman if a communication had been received referring to the proposed provision of a dock in the vicinity of Duke's Fields. If a letter had been received be would like to know what information, if any, was given upon the subject.—The Chairman ad- mitted that a letter had been received but it would not be wise to disclose its contents.—The minutes were adopted as amended.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The recommendations of this Committee were that the tender of Mr. J. Green for painting, Sto., to be done at the hospital for £2 2. 6d. be accepted. That Mr. E. Gregory's tender for the supply of provender for the next six months be accepted. fhat Mr. Joshua Fradley, Lowland's-road,be registered as a purveyor of milk. That notices be served upon the owners of property situated 7,9,11,13, and 15 Mersey-street, 2,46,8, and 10 Canal- street to abate certain nuisances, and in the event of non-compliance with the same legal proceedings be tsken. That the inspector of nuisances be in future appointed permanently, subject to good behaviour ; that the terms of the appointment be in other respects the same ; and that the necessary steps be taken to carry out this re- solution. The sanitary inspector had reported to the committee as follows :—" On the 11th May having noticed a paragraph in one of the evening papers to the effect than an Italian woman and her baby had been re- moved to the small pox hospital in %Farrington and that she had come from Runcorn I made inquiries and found that she had been lodging at Murphy's in Mersey-street and had come from Northwich to e rodsham and then to Runcorn. lat once thoroughly disinfected the bedroom bedding, &c." Mr. Imison proposed the con- firmation of the minutes with the exception' of the one referring to the appointment of inspector of nuisances which required amending. He would, therefore, suggest that he give notice that day of his intention to move at the next meeting of the Board that Mr. James Percival Ifould be elected inspec- tor of n.:!sances at a salary of £125 per annum, subject to the appointment terminating at a month's notice, and that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction.—Mr. Grice seconded, and it was car- ried.

div.head: LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

Among the recommendations of this Commitree was one that the vacancy on the Committee created by the retirement of Mr. William M. Sowerby be filed up.— Mr. Handley proposed that the minutes be confirmed, and that time Rev. John Simpson be selected to fill the vacancy.—Mr. Grice seconded, and the proposition was agreed to.
SIIIPWRIGEITS AND TILE GRAVING DOCK IitIESTION.

The Chairman announced that he had received the following letter bearing upon the above question. "19, Egerton-st., Runcorn, May 21st, 1894, Sir,—At a joint- meeting of painters, shipwrights, and boilermakers held on May 19,in St. JOhn s room it was resolved unan- imously that I communicate with the chairman of the Commissioners requesting him to receive a joint deput L- .tion of the same .espectine• the graving dock question. A reply as early as possible will oblige. A. Ravenscrieft • secretary.' Continuing, Mr. Taylor remarked that a reply had been sent informing the writer that the Board would.cominuniaate further with him upon the question. He (the chairman) now suggested that the letter be re- ferred to the Gencral Purposes Committee who were at present dealing with the matter.—Mr. Bisbrown said lie was glad that the trades had taken this action and he moved that the letter be referred to the Committee. He would like to bnow if a reply had been received from the canal company concerning the , proposed provision of a graving dock.—Mr. Lake replied in the negative. Mr. Handley seconded the proposition, being, of this opinion that the men ought to have an opportunity of stating their views. He had had conversations with many members of both trades, and had found that the feeling existed that the Commis- sioners were not doing as much as they ought to do in the matter. It was therefore desirable that the public should know that the Board ware doing their utmost for the best interests of the inhabitants of the town gener- ally.—Mr. Speakman supported, but suggested that the deputation should meet the General Purposes Committee. —Mr. Bisbrown accepted the suggestion.—The Chair- man said he had had a conversation with the Chairman of the General Purposes Committee,and he had intended to call a meeting together to meet the deputation.—Mr. Once thought that as it was a question which affected the interests of the town to such an extent, it should be dis- cussed by a Committee of the whole Board. Be himself, would like to hear the arguments advanced by the deputa- tion.—The Chairman did nol think there was any objec- tion to this proceeding,and several of the members were also of this opinion.7-Mr.lmison proposed that the meet- ing be held in the evening which which was agreed to.— The amended proposition was then put and carried. ,

div.head: DIVISION- OF THE DISTRICT INTO WARDS.
div.p: THE DIVISION- OF THE DISTRICT INTO WARDS.

The Chairman said thWt the County Council had sup- ported their request for the division of Runcorn into wards, and It has been passed.—Mr. Meadowcroft asked if the Clerk could give the Board any inrormation m- garding the probable cost which Runcorn would be put to under the Registration Bill now before Parliament. He had seen in the papers the estimate for Lancashire, and he would like to know that of Cheshire, and how much of this would fall upon Runcorn. The Clerk re- plied that he had no such information at his disposal.

THE QUESTION 01' PUBLIC BATHS. Mr. Handley said that this question had not been lost sight of. The committee had held a meeting, and were holding another next week when something of a detinate natme would be most likely reported.

div.head: MAINTENANCE Or MAIN ROLM
div.p: THE MAINTENANCE Or MAIN ROLM

The Chairman informed the meeting that & letter had been received from the Cheshire County Council to the effect that the sum of £2OO allowed the Board for main- tenance of main roads would be increased in future to £4OO. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Speakman considered that it was necessary now to keep account of every penny spent because the Council would require a detailed statement. He therefore suggested that a sub-commit- tee of three be appointed to act with the Surveyor.—Mr. Pritchard seconded.—Mr. Speakman said that although a fixed amount had not been stated yet he thought they would experience no difficulty, if they made a good case, to get a little more should their expenditure exceed the £4oo.—Mr. Imison thought. it was unwise of the Board to take business which was not named upon the agenda, and that the Committee would be able to manage the matter themselves.—Mr. Speakman said he did not wish to press the matter so long as the suggestions named by him were carried out, and consequently withdrew his motion.

div.head: MR. LEACH ENTERS A PROTEST.
div.p: MR. LEACH ENTERS A PROTEST.

Mr. Leach said -he Would resign his position as Chair- man of the Markets Committee in protest against the action of the Finance Committee with reference to the increase of salary granted to the market inspector. The Markets Committee brought forward the recommenda- tion that the increase be granted, but this was referred to the Finance Committee who imposed other duties uprin Mr. Garrett for which he was to be remuner- ated at the rate of £lO per year. fie, had always understood that a Committee had control of the servants engaged in their department.—Several mem- bers expressed regret that Mr. Leach had determined to resign the chairmanship of the Committee in which posi- tion he had always manifested such an active interest and had done such good service. Many of the reasons for such an action were very slender and of a sentimen- tal character, merely being a matter of feeling. It was also pointed out that the questien of salary had to finally come before the Finance Committee. In the case al- luded to,if the Markets Committee had persisted in their recommendation their servant would ry.t have had his remuneration increas 1, whereas by filling up his time in copying out the rate book, a way had been found to give him the nroposed increase which was satisfactory to the Market Inspector and the ratepayers. Therefore, the hope was expressed by many that by the next Board meeting, Mr. Leach would have re.coosidered his deci. pitm to retire. g • This terminated *proceedings,
A BICYCLE ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN,

div.head: CLAD' FOR DA!%IAGES.
div.p: CLAD' FOR DA!%IAGES.

; At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, :before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, and a ! . jury, john Bentham, 88 Legh-at., Earlestown, sued , Richard B. Toft,grocer,l9, Bridge-st.,Earles;own, for , £lOO for injuries alleged to have been inflicted by the defendant knocking him down by a bicycle in Market-st., Earlestown, on January 2nd of the pre- sent year. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Longton defended. Mr. Browne, in opening the case, said that the plain- tiff was a collier and received from is. to 84. per day. He was 66 years of age. He received some very serious injuries in consequence of Mr. Toft running into him with his bicycle on January 2nd, while crossing from , one side of Market-st., ts the other. The street was about ten yards in width. The plaintiff was almost across the street when he was suddenly knocked down by the bicycle, which struck him in a dangerous place. The plaintiff contended that he was not to blame as he . had a perfect right to use the road, and on Hie other hand, the defendant had no right to go the reckleas pace with which bicyclists had lately given way to. The de- fendant was also on the wrong side of the road. The bicycle fell on the top of the !AL intiff, who also received an injury upon his foot. After the accident had t iken place, the defendant said to the plaintiff " Old man, I thought I had killed you." The plaintiff replied, " You have not killed me, but you have lamed me for life." ' The defendant then said tl:.a.:, if his icycle had had an iron wheel, it would have.split the plaintiff in two. The i defendant then offered to take him to a doctor, hut lie I asked to be taken home. Ile was taken into the Market 4 Hotel, and defendant left some money for some brandy, 4 and the plaintiff was subsequently taken home. He had been in bed for 12 or 13 weeks. The defendant sent his own doctor to attend Bentham, and it was not until i seven weeks before Bentham had a doctor of his own. ; He had to be poulticed, and fox-sometime was unable to ! feed himself. It had ty!en said that the plaintiff had , been a maling,erer, but he would bring evidence to prove that that was not se. He would also bring independent witnesses who saw tile accident who would prove that the plaintiff was absolutely unable to get out of the way._

folin Bentham the plaintiff, then gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement. He said that he never heard any bell ring, and did not see the bicycle coming. He never refused to get out of bed when told by Dr. Valentine who attended him. He had never worked since the accident, and when the weather -was damp, he was always affectel lie had been attended by Dr.. Hayward since Dr. Valentine had ceased to attend him. —Cross examined ; He and Toft were going in oppo- site directions when the bicycle ran into him. He never grasped the bicycle with his hands. Mr. Toft was not sitting on his bicycle for some time after the accident occurred. Mr. Longton was proceeding to question the plaintiff upon his previous illnesses, but his Honour said that he could not see what this had to do with the case. Mr.Longton said that he was questioning the credibility of the plaintiff, and then aeked whether he had not left several places in debt. His Honour again interrupted, and said that he could not see what on earth that had to do with the case.

John Massey, van man, 54, Sankey-street, Earlestown, said that on January 2, he was 'delivering bread in Market-street. Ho saw Mr. Toft conaing 'along on a bicycle towards Haydock, at a great pace. He watched him, and when he got about. 20 yards from where witness was standing, 13enthem came across the road, and was about to step on the parapet, when Toft "ran into " him, and knocked him three or four yards. Bentham fell flat on his back. He saw Toft and a man named Sherlock take Bentham into the Market Hotel. There was a clear space in the road when the accident occurred. Toft was on the right hand side of the read when the accident occurred. -

William Lord, collier, 53, Houghton-street, Etries- town, said that he was in Nlarket-street on January 2nd. Be saw Toft going up Market-street. Witnoss was about 30 yards from where the accident occurred. He corro- borated last witue.,:s.

Ellen Bentham, the platntiff's wife, said that she and Mrs. Price undressed her husband when he got home. He was in great pain, and they fomented him with hot water and fllnnels. The injured parts were very black and swollen:—Ellen Price, 103, Legh-street, Earlestown, corroborated the last witness.

—Roger Wood and Dr. Hayward each gave evidence on behalf of the plaintiff, the latter stating that he ex- amined plaintiff on February 21, who complained of pain which might have been caused by the injuries com- plained of. _ _ _

- Mr. Longton for the defence argued that Bentham ought to have seen the bicycle coming, and had therefore, contributed by his negligence to the accident. Mr. Taft asserted that he rang the bell, and the accident would not have occurred had not the plaintiff rushed across the street, and ran into the bicycle. Mr. Taft could not help running into him. Mr. Toft was ex- tremely sorry for the accident and some ti:ne ago, he had offered £5 to settle tir:e case. The injury was inflicted by an indiarubber wheel which however, would never hare gone on the top of the plaintiff had he not caught hold of the wheel and pulled it over him. lie was mot thrown on his back, but simply in a sitting position, and a conversation ensued. The plaintiff declined to see a doctor, hut said he would have some brandy for which Mr. Taft paid. Mr. Taft never sent any doctor to see the plaintiff. As for the plaintiff stopping in bed since the accident, he was suffering from lumbago from which be frequently suffered. He did not suffer from the acci- dent more than a week.
No further evidence was heard, the case being ad- journed until next Thursday.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF THE HAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD CLERK.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF THE HAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD CLERK.

The people of Haydoek, and more especially the Members of the Llcal Board are much conlerned over the disappearance of Mr. J. Matthews, the Clerk to the Board, which has deepened into one of profound mystery. Mr. _Matthews with his wife resided at the house attached to the Board's offices,ana last Tuesday morning he left home, without giving any in- dication to his wife or relatives as to his destination. On Thursday owing to nothing being heard of his where- abouts, enquiries were set on foot, and a special meeting of the Board was held. This meeting was called to con- sider the course to he adopted the following day at the 1. County Council enquiry into the question of dividing tho township into wards. Mr. Matthews failed to attend this meeting, and he did not put in an appearance at the enquiry. His relatives became much concerned, and his father having heard that he had gone to Cork, proceeded there, but failed to wain any tidings of his son. On Friday a man named Armstrong who lives at Ashton said he had seen him on Crewe station, having just left the London train, and that he entered another train for Liverpool, but nothing further could be learned of him. Enquiry has since been made in every direction, but not the faintest clue can be obtained, and his disappear- ance so far is shrouded in mystery. Up to the present there is no suspicion that any harm has befallen tin%

_ The Board met again on Monday, and instructed Mr. R. Bradshaw (accountant) and Mr. E. J. George to make an examination of the books. The investigation was completed on Wednesday, the lesult being in every way satisfactory, in fact the accounts show .a balance in Mr. Matthews' favour. Some tiroe ago Mr. Matthews suffered in health, and was attended by Dr. Dowling,and lately a nervous disorder has developed itself alarmingly and it is feared that this may to some extent account for his strange disappearance. The duties are at present being performed by Mr. John Baines.

div.head: NEW CLERK APPOINTED.
div.p: NEW CLERK APPOINTED.

Mr. Grimk6.l) rayton presided on Thursday at the meeting of the riaydock Local noard, and in addition there were present Messrs. E. J. George, secretary to Messrs. Evans and Co., and R. Bradshaw, late account- ant, to that firto, who had gone through the accounts of Mr. John Matthews, the clerk to the hoard,who has been missing since Tuesday, May 29. Mr. Charnock from the offices of Messrs. Peace and Ellis. law clerks, Wigan.was also present. The Chairman said it would simplify mat ters if they appointed Mr. Bradshaw clerk,pro tem. As chairman he thanked Mr. Bradshaw for the trou He he had taken in going through the accounts and putting things straight. Mr. Bradshaw having signified his willingness to accept the post, Mr. Jackson moved and Mr. John Turton seconded that Mr. Matthews, the missing clerk, he suspended, and that Mr. Bradshaw he appointed to the office pro. fem. This was carried unanimously. The Chairman said the representatives of the Press would gather at once that the accounts had been gone into,and that the books and figures were nr4perly balanced. There was no question shout money. Mr. Bradshaw then read a statement of affairs showing that the cash account had been writt-n up by Mr. nitthews to the 3rd of January. HP had gone through the hooks since then, and as far as he could find out there was a balance owing to Mr. Matthews of money raid by him in wages, petty cash, &c., of £36 85.10 d. The Board passed a re- solution requesting the hank to honour Mr. Bradshaw's cheques. The routine business was then procerded with. Up to the present there are no tidings of Mr. Matthews.

div.head: ST. HELENS
div.p: ST. HELENS

Tllll PROPOSED NEW WATERWaRKS. f The Local (iovernrnent Board has agreed to allow the St. Helens Corporat)ou thirty-eight years in which to repay the money proposed to be borr. wed for the con- striction of new waterworks at Melling, near Orms- ki, Ir. The cost of the scheme is estimated at £75.000.

HOLY CROSS CHURCH. At St. Helens Police Court on Tuesday, Mr. Meary applied Cu bchalf of Mr. J,41-in Bellis, of the A 1 public house, for an occasional license for four days next week for an outdoor fete on behalf of the fund for re-roofing Holy Cross Church. Mr. Alearns said the applicant would m no profit for himself, all the profits of the !fete goNg to the church funds.--The application Was granted.

THE BOLD HALL ESTAI7II. uNderstand that at the rent audit of the aid Hall Estate Company, St. Helens, on :thursday week, thh tanners were allowed 10 per cent. on their rents for ne past half year. The audit was held at the ripping Arms Hotel, Bold, where a substantial dinner was provided for the farmers. The reduction is allowed pending the completion of the extnisive repairs to the farms, which have been of lat., much neglected.

PROPOSED PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY. A fleeting of persons interested in the formation of a photographic society in Bt. Helens WPS held at the Fleec)'i Hotel on Monday. The Rev. J. W. Willink M.A., vicar, presided, and first spoke of the general -advantar.fes of photography, and then a discussion ensued. It WRi ultimately decided to form a club, which should be open to amateurs or professionals, with ladies as members, and a committee was appointed to draft rulesand make such arrangements as were necessary.

APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. The Parliamentary and Health Corninitteas of the A Helens Corporation have appointed Dr. John R.ibertson. at present assistant medical officer of health, to succeed Dr. APNicoll, the medical officer, who has retired. The Committees recommend the Council to fix the salary of Dr. Robertson as £4OO, rising by five equal annual in- stalments to £5OO. The new medical officer is required to devote the who'e of his time to the duties of the office. Toe appointment is subject to confirmation by the Coun- cil on Wednesday next.

FOUND DROWNED. At the St. Helens Town Hall on Thursday, Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of a man at present unknown, which was foiind floating ors Tuesday night, in the S. Helens and Sankey Canal near the central ofEces of the United Alkali Company. In- spector Steele stated that the body was dressed in a brown tweed coat aril vest, blue flannel singlet, blue and white cotton shirt, brown tweed trousers, red and black pocket handkerchief round neck, dark grey socks and clogs. There was nothing on the body to lead t, identification. The body appeared to be that of a laboui- ing man, aged about forty-five. There were no marks or bruises on the body, with the exception of one or two caused by getting it out of the water. The body was sft. 10in. long and the face was clean shaven, with dark moustache. A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.

LOCAL VETO MEETING AT PRESCOT. A highly-successful gathering of working men in sup 4 port of the above bill took place on Wednesday evening,. " in the open air, on the Old Park, Prescot, The meeting, which was under the auspices of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Direct Veto League, was presided over by Mr.Frecr. W. Hall (secretary to the organisation), Mr.Ed.Boreland (district superintendent, United liingdiqo Alliance),and Mr. Morris Jones (district secretary, South-West Lanca- shire District Lodge, Independent Order of Good Temp- tars) being the principal sneakers. A petition in favour • of the Government Veto Bill, and urging the reintroduc- tion of the measure without further delay, was unanit mously adopted, a copy to be signed by the chairman; and forwarded to Mr. A. B. Forwood,M.P.,for presenta- tion to the House of Commons. Messrs. A. Francis (St: Helens) and J. Lindon (Prescot) also participated in the proceedings.

LIBERAL MEETING. In connection with the ward meetings which ans being promoted by the St. Helens Liberal Association,, a meeting was held- on Monday night, in the schools at Micklehead Green. The district is a scattered one on the extreme boundary of the borough, and contains about 150 or ZOO electors. Mr. G. W. Rawlins presided', and was supported by Councillor John Forster, J.P., and Mr. W. Seath. The Chairman said he looked upon the present Government as the best Liberal Government the- country had ever seen, and he hoped they would have an opportunity of sending to the House of Lords the measures the country had made up its mind during the last ten years to have. (Applause.)—Mr. Seath pro- posed a resolution expressing confidence in the Govern- ment, and pressing them t continue their great work hi spite of opposition.—Counefflor Forster, in seconding the resolution, said the Government had kept plodding on, and to-day they could present a clean sheet as to the promises they made at the last election.—The resoluticn was carried unanimously, and votes of thanks to the speakers and to the chairman closed the meeting.

A LLECIED MALICIOUS rROSECUTION. Judge Shand and a jury heard an action at the St. Helens County Court on Wednesday for damages for malicious prosecution brought by :Tames Platt against Samuel Williams. Both men were miners at Eccle,tata Hall Colliery, where a custom prevails of leaving picks in a smithy to be sharpened. Platt somehow became possessed of Williams picks, but restored them as soon as asked. Williams laid a police information. alleging that Platt had stolen them. As, however, EccleAan Hall Colliery was not in the borough of St. Helens, although the parties both reside in Vie borough, the Case collap- sed and Williams did not proceed further with the case, as he might have done, in the county division, Mr. Riley,for the plaintiff, contended that if a man was mali- ciously put to trouble at any time that was a ca'rong which was answerable by damages.—Mr. Malden, for the defence, said Williams acted in the belief that his picks were stolen.—Defendant, in answer to Mr. Riley, said he would have been satisfied, after taking out the summons, if PlaV., had paid him one day's wage.—The Judge said that if the summons was tk .n out in order to coerce Platt to par there was no jostification.—The jury considered that Platt had no intention of stealing the pick+, and awarded him £2 damage and £2 18s. the costs of the police court defence.

div.head: ALLNGED KICKING OUTRAGE.
div.p: ALLNGED KICKING OUTRAGE.

On Tuesday, before Alderman Mitir;:de, Councillor James Buret all, Messrs. W. J. Thomson, B. B. Glover, and T. Glover, Thomas M'Cue surrendered to his bail charged with unlawfully wounding Maria Carney, hy kicking her on the lower part of the body on the 28th April. Chief Constable Wood conduced the proceedings., and Mr. 11. L. Riley defended. Mrs. Carney, whose in- juries had been of a terrible nature, was in a weak con- dition, and was accommodated with a seat. She said she was a widow, fifty years of age. On the 28th of April last she was living at 25, Wright-street, with her son, John Carney. Abut eleven o'clock that night sl e heard a noise at the corner of Wright-street and Potter - street, and on going there she found pris.oner and her son fighting. John was lying on the ground,and prisoner was over him. She asked prisoner not to kill him, and asked two other men to bring him home. They did not respond, and she stoopel down to lift up her son, when prisoner gave her a kick in the lower part of the body. She was badly injured, but managed to scramble to her own house. She was unconsci•an for four days.—Dr. Jameson, who with Dr. Knowles and Dr. Potter was called, described the terrible injuries of the woman. Witness had never heard of a similar case. There was noexternal injury. Nothing as more likely to mien the injury than a kick, hut the case was such an ex- traordinary one that lie would not say positively it was caused by a kick.—Mr. Riley suggested that the woman had strained herself by slipping while stooping. Very few people, the doctor adnaitt.d, would dream of such possibilities as this from a kick which left no mark ex. ternally.—Police-sergeant Sisson, who arrested prisoner, said the latter declared he was not guilty, and had not seen Mrs. Carney.—Prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—Two elnquent germ Mfg trrre delivered on Sunday afternoon and evening by the Rev. J. C. Jowett, of Dinsbury, in the Halton Wesleyan Church. Large congregations were present, and the services were much enjoyed. On Monday evening another service WaS held, at which the Rev. J. Hanby presided. Special hymns and pieces were rendered a!•,-. each service by the children and choir, under the atilt/ leadership of Mr. H. Hone, junr., whilst Mr. R. Sutton presided at the organ. The collections, which were. in aid of the Sabbath School, realized 03. It might be added that the total number of officers and teachers is twenty-seven, whilst the total number of scholar on the books is 286. The annual cost of the schools is £2B, so that it will he seen that the sch,ol should possess a balance of £5 towards the next year's fund.

A WARRINGTON HAWKER IN A LEIGH COVET. At the Leigh Petty Sessions,- on Moiel,,y, William Smith, hawker, Warrington, was placed it the dock on a charge of stealing a lead pump, value 10s., belonging - to Peter Cleworth, VicarageFarm,Westleigh,between the 26th August and the 3rd October last.—Peter Cieworth uaid schon he missed the articles he gave information to the pelice. He could not swear that prisoner was the mar be ea o knocking about the premises between the dates in question.—Patrick Riley, labourer, 9, Canal- utreet, Penningfon,said at the time prisoner was lodging with him and his mother. They went hawking to- gether during the time mentioned, going t. Vicarage Farm. Prisoner got a pump from somewhere. When Lie got to his lodgings, the pump was put in the back 7ard and covered with bricks. Prisoner told witness to uay nothing about it.—P.C.Bishop saUd he arrested pHs- ener at Warrington on the 28th ult, Out he said he knew nothing about the matter. He now made the defence.— He was dismissed. the Bench not being satisfied that be was the right man. AN I72ROAR AT THE BARRACKS. Monday was the day for the assembling t-af the Liver- pool Militia at Orford Barracks. and one sequel to it was, the bringing before the borough magistrates on Tuesday, four militiamen, for being drunk and disorderly, 'in Marstihouse-lane, and also with assaulting the police. Their names were John Langford, 12, Cartwright-street. Liverpool; Samuel Swift, 66, Oliver-street. Liverpool ; Lewis Dowell, 17, Oleveria-street, Liverpool. and Daniel Farley, Warren-street, Liverpool. The first three named prisoners were charged with the assault upon the pclice. PC. Bruen stated that a number of drunken militiamen entered the barrack,?, the previous morning, and several of them were turned nut, including the prisoners. An order was given at 1.30. not to admit any more into the barracks, and about 300 congregat.d round the yard gate. 'They commenced shouting and tried to I,,iet into the harrx.ka yard. Some pickets were urnt to the assistance of the police to keep order. At two o'clock two coat carts came to the barracks, and wherethey were entering the gates,the first and third prisoners (Langford. and Howell) made a rush at P.C.'s Barlow and :k.fewey and knocked them down and kicked them . . The prisoner swift drew a bayonet from one of the soldiers' sides,and would have done some injury bad it not been knocked out of his hand. P.C.'s Barlow and Newev gave evid- ence as to the assaults upon them. Swift was sent to gaol for six weeks, Langford and Howell one month each, and Farley, fourteen days' imprisontn.nt. THEFT OF Fowls AT EARLESTOWN.

At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday. Benjamin Haynes, bricklayer's labourer. 17, Alliert-s., Warrington, was charged with stealing three fowls,from the henpen on the farm, War.Trave-road. Newton, on Saturday, the 26th ult., valued at 64., the property of Mrs. Sarah Pritchard. Prisoner pleaded not entity. Mr. Pritchard, con of the complainant, stated that on the night of the date named, from some information he received, he went to a passage leading to the E irlestown Railway Station, and there found on the ground a work- rnan's bass containing two hens and a piece of pork,ani another hen tied in a blue handkerchief. There was no .-ne in possession of them,but he heard someone running down the passage. The hens were dead but inhe warm and they were the property of his mother.—E len Berry, domestic servant in the employ of Mr. Slee, Wargrave- road, Newton, stated that she went on business to the farm, and whilst going through the yard she heard a noise in the henpen. On returning she saw two men near the railway passage, and one of them was killing a -hen. On seeinc her they. ran away. File returned to the farmhouse and told Mrs. Pritchard.—Ellen A.liton. wife of William Ashton, 26, Lawrence-street. Earlestewn, deposed that the prisoner for a short time lodged her, a,nd she had seen him in possession ot the t.a4s pro- duced.—Richard Morris, landlord of the Sulthr am fen, Wargrave-road. gave evidence as to the prisener at his house on the night of the date named.—Sergeant Longworth stated that from information he received. he concealed himself in the railway passage. The prisener came up to where the bass lay, hut aftcr ~-nne hesitation, he turned away and did not pick it up. Witness took his name and address, which was after- wards found to have been given incorreetly.—'.C. Schofiela spoke ;as to apprehending the priconer. lii reply to the charge of stealing the fowl he replied " had nothing to do with them." The prisoner ar first denied having been in Earlestown. Ile was committed to gaol for one month. The charge of stmling pork was not proceeded with. A WARRINGTON ERI,FIA.N.

Thomas Bagguley, Pump-yard, was charged at the Warrington Borous.da Court on Monday with uaiawfully nutting and wounding Patrick Cerßeid, who, lives in the same yard, at 7 30, on Saturday :evening, with intent to inflict grievous bodily injury. The Chief Coost4tile ste ed that tin, complainant and a man named Shaw, went into the Vine 'cavern on Satnrclar' aft irnnon. at about four o'clock, and each had a glass of beer. Some- time afterwards, prisoner came into the house and got a glass of beer, and then endeavoured to make a quarrel with Cortield, the result of which being that the prisoner was ejected from the house. At about 7.30 the same night. Cnrtield was standing at the entrance to Pumn-yard 'having a stMke, when the prisoner came up, and knocked the pipe out of his mouth, and 'wed Pirtle threats. He then inppeil Corfield in the mouth with his head. Ile was nest seen to take a knife out of his pocket and strike Cerfeed in the eye with it with a hack-handed blow. Corfield's son at this point came up and senara.ted them, and he tre- k ' his father to the Infirmary. Corfield lost a larre quantity of blood. Information was given to the police, and Bagguley was locked up on the present charge. When charged with the assairlt. the prisoner said that he had inflicted the wonnd with a ring which was on his finger.—Patrick Cortield gave corroborative evidPnee in support of the Chief Constable's statement.—Dr.new. den, the house sureeon for the Infirmary, said that the complainant was ndmiteed into the In. firmary on Saturday night suffering from a lacerated wound in the left eyelid. The eyelid was completely divided. There was also a contusion en the eyeball. The wound was probably caused by a. pointed instrument •which was not very sharp. He did not think the eye- sight would he injured.—John Corfield, the son of the 'complainant, said that he saw the prisoner pull a knife out of his pocket and strike Corfield in the eyp with it. Afterwards when trying to separate the two parties, witness received a slight wound on the linger 'cc-Ph the knife.—Atter further evidence by Annie Corfield and Detective Monaghan, the prisoner made a statement, to the effect that the complainant struck him first, and denied that he ever used a knife. He was Colllllll,tted tO the Liverpool Assizes.

The evidence of, the corn- plainaet was that she had a quarrel with the defendant about some private affairs, and at length the defendant struck her in the face. A number of witnesses were called on either side and the evidence was so conflicting that the magistrates dismissed the case.—Mary Jane Wright, 77, Rewsey-street, was charged with assaulting Sarah Ann Walsh, Catherine-street. on May 27. The complainant said that the defendant hit her with A chair in consequence of a dispute over family affairs. 'The de- fendant denied the 'assault and brought witnesses to prove her assertion. She was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and pay the costs.—Emma Jane Smith, Pierpoint-street, was Charged with using threats to Sarah Ann Wright. the defendant in the last case, on May 23. The case was dismissed. each side to pay their costs. , AN UNSUPPORTED CHAROE.—Henry Turner. jun., 22. Dallam-lane, was charged with assaulting Alice Taylor, 26 Dallatn-lane. on May 27. The complainant said that she was going down the entry behind ber house when the defendant called her a bad name, and struck her in the face. She called the defendant's sister as a witness, but this person denied that any assault whatever had been committed by the defendant. The magistrates ac- cordingly dismissed the case, Alderman Francomb re- marking that if the defendant was as quiet outside as he was in the:box.he would not get up many rows. DISPUTE OVER A WlLL—William Hunt. 23. Chester-st., was summoned by his brother James Hunt,3l,Ly thgoes- lane,for using threats on May 27. The defendant pleaded guilty. The complainant said that the defendant came into his yard on the above date, and commenced using threats to him. His brother had been struck out of his father's will because he had struck his father,ancl he and his mother were now trying to strike him(James) out The defendant denied that he had struck his father at all. The magistrates hoped that the brothers would become friends again,and as William expressed his willingness to be bound over, they adopted this course. and on going out of the court, the brothers shook hands with each other.

The defendant did not ap- pear, but was represented by his mother.—The Chief Constable said that the defendant had been throwing stones at another boy taut missed the bov and hit Weir with such force that the stone cut through his hat and made a serious wound in his head.—Weir said that .he did not wish to press the catte, and if he had known who had thrown the stone, the case would never have come into the court.—The magistrates dismissed the case and hoped that defendant's mother would give her son a good talking to.

D.S. Winaghan qlpped him, and found the shirt produced under the prisoner's coat. He asked him what account he had ta give about it, and the prisoner replied that he was at the stores at the Barracks, and had the shirt thrown at him. He was taken ta the Police Station, and it was further found that he was wearing the military socks produced. On being charged with stealing the articles he replied "I had them given me." Two officers stared tt-at the pri- soner had no right to have the articles in his possession. D.S. Monaghan gave evidence as to arresting the pri- soner, who had made two statements about the articles. He at first stated that Colour-Sergeant Feeney had given the articles to him, and afterwards that a private named Makin had given them him. He was sent to gaol for three weeks' hard labour.

The evidence of the complainant and -his wife, was to the effect that on the night of the date named one of their windows was broken by the throwing of rotten eggs, which they alleged-was -done by the defendants, although they did not see them throwing. The defen- dants admitted being there at the time, but denied throwing. The magistrates ordered them to pay 2s. 'damages and DORIS. UNFRIENDLY NElGHBORS.—Elizabeth Bay, 'Howard- street, Sankey Bridges,was charged with using threaten- ing languatre to Sareh Atkin, a neighbour residing in .the same street, on the 28th ult. Mr. A. Browne, solici- tor, appeared on behalf of the complainant. < The com- plainants case was that on the date named she was asked by the defendant "to stand her; a pint" which she refused to do. A " row " ensued in which the de- fendant broke a window of the complainants, threw a flower pot at the complainant —which missed her and Struck her brother on the head, and also used threaten- ing language to the complainant. Mrs. Atkin was now afraid of the defendant. Corroborative evidence was given by William Burgess and Joseph 'lumen- The de- fendant denied the charges, and called two neighbours in support of her statement, named Mrs. Blease, Barnet- street, Sankey Bridges, and Mre. Jordan, 95, Howard- street. The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months in a surety of £lO. WARNING TO BO&TMEN.—Williarr: Lloyd, a boatman, wee charged with having on the 17th April at Burton- wood, used a canal boat without having had the same registered. Mr. Kerfoot, nuisance inspector for the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority,stated that on the 17th ult. he was on the canal bank and saw the defen- dant in charge of a canal boat. He asked him whether he had been registered to which he replied that he was registered by the Customs Authority, Liverpool. Wit- ness wrote to Liverpool the same night inquiring as to the truth of the defendant's statement, and he received a reply that the defendant was not registered with them. The defendant was unable to produce his certificate. In his statement to the magistrates, the defendant said that he had been registered, but had lost his certificate some years ago. He was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: COMIC CRICKET MATCH AT EA RLES-
div.p: COMIC CRICKET MATCH AT EA RLES-
TOWN.

For the purpose of assisting the funds of the Earlestown Cricket Club and the Viaduct Institute brass band, a cricket match was played on the Earlestown ground on Saturday afternoon.betweeu the first eleven of the Eariestown Club and twenty- four tradesmen and others of the town. The cricketers played with broomsticks, but their opponents used the ordinary willow. Tao "Comics," for suh they styled themselves, had gone to a lot of trouble and ex- pense in preparation for what they expected to be a gala day,but Jupiter Pluvius,who was not chosen to play, but had an innings on his own account, and sent forth during the whole f-if the afternoon ,an uncomfortably. large number of drenching showers of rain,which some- what damped the ardour, and spoiled the finery of the "Comics." It did not, however, debar a very large number of people from putting in an appearance to witness the fun, although had "Old Sol" been on his best behaviour, there is no doubt the attendance would have been very much larger, and the funds proportion- ately enhanced. lo say that the " Comics", were not a motley crew would be to exaggerate, when it is stated that clowns and the " heathen Chinee " rubbed shoulders with such an Minor-ant personage as " Bel- phegor,"- while " John Bull " had friendly intercourse with " Ally Stoner." A " Scottish Chieftain " in kilt looked thoroughly out of place, but the sailor seemed quite in his element. The I,l4rlestown team batted first, hit all the laws of cricket were at once thrown to the w nds, and the decisions of umpires were treated with rhschin. if a player stayed too long he was promptly haedcuffed and walked MT to the pavilion to make room for another player. It was evident from the first that the " Comics " intended to win by any means, and they succeeded, for if they could not catch a ball in the ordin- ary way, they caught it in a top hot. The match was most amusing,especially when if a player became obstre- perous, the police ser•zeant, a youngster about 12 years old, had to take him in charge and settle all disputes by marching him off to the pavilion. When the comics went to the wickets, they intended to stay, and in some cases refused to be out, when given out by the umpire. John Bud and BOphegor " took the precaution to provide themselves with extending hits, with which they completely covered the wukets. The match haul however to he greatly ourtailed,and with only 13 wickets down, play was brought to a close in a soaking rain. The band was present and played one or two .eleetions of inuOc. "THE RIGHT TO WORt."

The Swiss people have been askld tn vote " yes " or " no" on the question whether, in their opinion, every: citizen willing to work but unable t.,) get etnoloynient had a 'right to have work found for him by the State. The answer was an emphatic " NO" ; 293,000 having voted against the obligation thus notiv,ht to be thrust upon the Executive, whilo onlv 75,00) were in favour of it. Th. Socialists had obtained 52,337 sieliatures to a petition for a referendum or plebiscite on the question. : .

div.p: REACHEROUS CONDUCT. IN SOUTH AFRICA.

The Criminal Court at Buluwayo has dealt with.the r^marlotbie charge preferred against two members of the Bechuanaland police force, of intercepting Lobengu- la's peace offering. and thereby prolonging the war and ousing the death of the gallant • Wilson and his party. That prisoners were on .patrol duty when they met two of. the Matahele indunas, who informed them that Lobengula intended to sorrender and handed to them gold to the va!ue of £l,OOO as a peace offering. The scoundrels pocketed the mowey and withheld the message, and the direct consequcmce was the loss of son's detachment. The Court found the prisoners guilty and sentenced them to penal servitude for fourteen years. In view of the peculiar circumstances it would not have been surprising had the prisoners been summarily exe- cuted.

div.head: sr. BABNABAS' NATIONAL SCHOOLS, WARRINGTON. BAZAAR AT THE GYMNASIUM,
div.p: sr. BABNABAS' NATIONAL SCHOOLS, WARRINGTON. BAZAAR AT THE GYMNASIUM,

An effort has recently been set on foot to raise funds to' meet the liability of the committee who guaranteed the hank for the balance of the building debt upon the St. Barnabas' Schools, Warrington, and also to pay for the street making and paving of the school yards. To meet these requirements, a sum of £250 was needed. A bazaar initiated for the purpose of raising this sum, v ns ononed in the Gymnasium, Palmyra Square, la mok„ There was a good number present at toe opening cere- money on Wednesday, and in addition to the Mavoress, there were also present—the Mayor(Alderman E. Green- all) the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), and Mrs. Willis, Rev. fI.V. and Mrs. Pigot, Rev. B. and Mrs. Percival, Rev. J.J. and Mrs. Langham, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton,Mr. and Mrs. T.Morris, Alderman Sutton, Councillor Smeth- urst, Mrs. Beamont, Mr. and Mrs. H. T. Smith, Mr. and Mrs. R. Proud, Mr. H. W. Cookson,Mrs. J. Harrison, Mr. W. A. Proud, Miss Pierpoint, Miss Westwell, Mrs. John White, Mr. Kinsley, etc. ! Mr. T. IMORUIS in introducing the Mayoress, said that ' it was pleasing to him to be present that afternoon, to help to realise enough money to pay off the debt hang- ing over the schools in St. Barnabas' parish. Be was • sure that every one present would do their utmost to aqain that object. fle.could not say anything in praise , of the Mayoress more than he had said a thousand times over before. She was always ready to assist in'every good work in the town, no matter what it was. She was no . respecter of persons so long as they were working for the good of the town. He was sure, that they would all spare no pains to make the bazaar a magnificent success. (Applause). _

• , The MAYORESS, who was received with applause, said that it gave her great pleasure to be there that day, and abe thanked them most heartily for the way in which they had received her. Having heard explained so fully the reasons for holding the bazaar, by Mr. Morris, little remained for her to say. The work which had been be- gun in that room, and would be continued during the following three days. was to raise £250, which was the amount required to clear off the debt at present existing unon the St. Itarnabas- Schools, which debt if not cleared then, would fall Upon the guarantors who so bravely came forward to take the responsibility upon themselves. (Hear, hear). Feeling as she did, the necessity in thr pi Os int day of assisting the schools in the district, she hau no hesitation in asking all present to do all they were able to do to assist in raising that sum to clear off the debt. In doing this, they would be assisting in the good object of helping to keep out of the town in the future as at presrnt,any fear of the School Board—(Ap- plause)—which would be the outcome of the lack of vol- untary support. She had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open, and trusted that double the sum required would b.! realised. (Applause). . . _

Alderman titer Tots Said that he felt it an honour to per- form the duty imposed upon him hy-Mr.Morris,which was to propose a hearty vote of thanks to the Mayoress, for her kindness in coming to open the bazaar that day. Since Mr. Greenall has become the Mayor of Warrington, the Mayoress bad always taken a very warm and active interest in everything which was for • the good of the town. She had been most indefatigable in her labours on behalf of every charitable institution. He was quite sure they would agree with him when he said that she had gained the esteem and good will of all classes of people in the town. (Applause.) He hoped the bazaar would be a success,and he asked them all to give a hearty vote of thanks to the Mayoress. He had to announce that Lady Greenall had, unfortunately, been unable to ' present at the bazaar. but Mrs. John White, who was present, had been deputed by Lady Greenall, to make purchases on her behalf. (Applause.) The RucTon seconded the vote of thanks. He agreed with all that was said about the 'Mayoress. With regard ' to theobject of the bazaar, he was sorry that there was a large di ht of :225U to he cleared. He house] it would: be cleared off. As the Mayoress had said, ho loped they • would be able to prevent the establishment of a School Board. He heartily endorsed that sentiment. The pre- sent time was a very critical time. Everything seemed to be against them, just at the time when they were re ceiving most valuable help from all quarters. He could not say how strongly he felt the importance of the work of the clergy and mansgers of the schools. They had no right to say that their schools were hetter than Board schools from a secular pniet of view, but theywere- better from a religious point of view. It was thOmun- den duty of the clergy and managers to see that the first hour's religious teaching was religiously kept. He had no sympathy with the clerey who did not attend or take an interest in their schools. But there were many who were doing all in their power to preserve their schools and make them thoroughly efficient. It was a difficult matter at the present time with all the additional re- quirements which goverement was making uoon them. but he firmly believed in Godeand if the cle rey did thelr duty, they would not be forsaken by the laity. The vote of thanks was carried with acclamation, and the Myron in replying for his wife, thanked them for the vote, and said that he had received great support from his wife in his public duties. He had an impar- taut engagement that afternoon which prevented his presence any longer. He hoptd that they would not think his absence was doe to any lack of interest in the bazaar, for he would leave his wife to make purchases on his behalf.

The businecs of the hazaar then commenced. The interior of the Gymnasimn had undergone a transforma- tion from its usual appearance,owing to the decorations consisting of bunting, artificial flowers, &c., which had beerr.artistically placed all over the building, by the workers undcr the supervision of NIA% Frank Proud, Mr. W. A. Proud, and Mr. H. Smith. There were six stalls 74:wed round the room, each of which was covered with articles of a useful and ornamental description. The followine, were the stalls and staPholdprs 1, Mrs. Morris, Mrs S. :Tones, Miss Coubrough, Miss L. Jones, Mi,ses Reid : No. 2, Mrs. Smith, Mrs. Smethurst, Mrs. Gorse, Mrs. Kent, Miss Smith, Misses Mills ; No. 3, Mrs. Proud, Mrs: Cupuage, Mrs. Cookson, Mrs.C.Bunch,Mrs. T. Needless • to say. this popular humorist was most enthusiastically received. Mr. T. Monnts in introduein4 him said that but for men lik.e Mr. Hebert • DAvies there would have been a School Board in ;,Varrington, which meant increased rates for the manufac,urera and shopkeepers to par, so that it was to the interest of penple in Warrinaton, to keep a School Board out of the town. They were al- ready heavily ra,ed, and the more they were rated the less people would come into Warrinr,ten, for high rates would not, cauqe goods to be sold cheaply. Mr. Robert Davies had always nobly come forward to help the Church of England out of their difficulty. Mr. Davms in declaring the bazaar open said .that having been both a Sunday sehort teacher and a school *manager, he felt great interest in matters of edneation.. There was no Christian denomination as far as he was aware, which desired to have education disseverel from religion. It was their dots' to seP that along- with .wQrldly knowledge, the higher knowledge should be given. In the next. place, .from - a financial point of view, ho coincided with the remarks of Mr. Morris. It would be a great misfottune to have a School Board, for Warrington was heavily burdened. Board schools wotild have to be built, for almost all those now used for educational purpesms, were also used as Sunday schools by the different. denominations who supported them, and they were also used for the choir practicer, ,ar,d other mectings. Therefore if a School Board were .eFtiblislied in Wartingtnn, there would have to he schools provided to meet the requirements ot the Educa- tion Department,. all over the town. The rates would he excessively high, and religious teaching which was at: present seen to by the clergy and ministers of the vari- ous denominations would have to be discontinued in its present form, He therefore hoped that when an effort such as the present was put ,forward, everyone of any denomination whatever would VOMA forward, and help them liberally. He was glad that the haz far had been a tolerable success to the pre virus day. He hoped it- would be the Fame that day and the followine. day. He had great pleasure in d‘ elating the bazaar noon. c,mncillor Se,ethurst proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Davies for perfnrmine the opening ceremony that after, _noon. With regard to the question of a Soho.' Board It" thought the inhabitants of Warrington were very lukewarm at present. At. the nresent time, they wow on the balance whether they should have a School Board at. not. 'Being a member of the School Attendance Committee, he was astonished how that committee were crushed in every .nook . and corner for extrmaiona and fresh aeenmino 'Winn.
