div.head: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL FINANCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL FINANCE.

As this matter has continued to attract a good deal of interest, our representative called upon Councillor Shaw Green and asked if he had any- thing further he would like to add in reply to the statements by the gentleman designated the "Busy Bee" in our last issue. Mr. Green said, "1 really do not see what there is in B.'s last article that demands .a reply. The statements are, now, oft-told tales that have been answered previously, and thougn anxious to give the ratepayers all the information po,ssible,one cannot flog a dead horse into vitality. One or two matters are, however, worthy of some recogni- tion. Mr. B. ,calls attention to page 215 of the borough treasurer's report. This report is up to March, 1893 only, and at that date there were six loans of the- old Waterworks still running. These have been re-arranged with the exception referred to in my previous observations, and with that ex- ception tee Corporation is now paying zio higher rate of interest than £3 ss. We have had many of these matters to deal with, but the loans were negotiated at a time when money was much dearer than now,and the cash was lent for .specific periods' It was only as they fell in that the re-arrangement could be made. Instead of imputing Llama and assuming that the Corporation was not able to deal with the financial matters, let me assert positively that the Corporation has endeavoured to fulfil the obligation it took over, and at the same time do its utmost in the interests of the ratepayers. This ought to be sufficient to satisfy the most captious critic, and after my emphatic statement it ought not to have been repeated, "With reference to the average rate of .E 3 6s. id. I disputed it altogether,and I quoted the rates now being paid, viz.; £3 ss. and £3 2sa6. As the higher rate is on a much greater sum than the smaller it could not be averaged without an immense amount of labour, but it is conclusive as , shewing that we are not paying £3 6s. id. "What doe* Mr. B. mean by the statement that the annuities are speculations and what does he mean by the further statement that it is anjundig- tidied way fox the Corporation to get money. "The annuities are sums equal to the interest paid on each share of the old Water Company and the, arrangements with the shareholders was that a cer- tain number ,of years purchase of this annuity should be the capital *value of each share. The amounts to be payable on the ordinary shares until 1896, when they are compulsorily redeemable and the amounts on the preference shares until 1,921 when they are compulsorily redeemable. Is tnis speculation? If so, Ido not know Where it comes in, the only .speculation that lean see is on the part of the public who may buy them, and certainly not on the part of the Corporation. Is it undignified? If so then the Corporation followed the example of the highest authority in the realm,vizathe Govern- ment tor what are known as Consols are really consolidated annuities. Thea the Mersey Dock Board has recently issued a very large amount of annuities, so that we are in good company if we are amongst the undignified. Then I want to know what is the good of twisting words 60 as to give them an entirely different meaning. Let anyola take the trauble to read the paragraph again and vermin) to -assert that none can conclude 1 said the water annuities could not be compulsorily re- deemable until 1921. I said a portion of them, viz., the annuities in lieu of the preference shares were not redeemable compulsorily until 1921. "A large part of the last article is taken up with a statement of what time Reading obtained in 1881. Of what possible use is this? I quoted 1882 as the date since which no period exceeding 60 years had been granted to a puolic Authority and to this period I must keep, for, as 1 pointed out, that prior to it we ourselves obtained 75 years to repay the gas purchase. "It may be in correcting the erroneous conclu- sions to which Mr. B. has arrived and by means of which he has endeavoured to show that the mem- bers of the Corporatian do not know their strength and are paying too high a rate of interest and a host of other things, that I have spoken out em- phatically for inyeelf and for the Corporation. It has been necessary- so to speak of what I know has been and is being done by that body, but where have I spoken for Parliament except to show the procedure? Such a paragraph as the one I refer to is Calculated to provoke stronger terms than the friendly replies to criticisms so misleading as Mr. B's.

"1 have however no doubt whatever it is in- teresting to the ratepayers to learn what the Finance Committee are doing. They have been trusted all along and are trusted still, and they will do all that business men ought or can do and when they come to offer their debenture stock they will seek to get as good terms as any othmr Corporation in the kingdom. 'Mr. B. has wasted a lot of energy in prov- ing that which is admitted viz.: That it is pos- sible either by a provisional order of the Local Government Board or by Parliamentary Authority for a local body to issue a debenture stock. This .1 again admit, but I assert that it is imperative lira to get the powers, and this we are taking the nec- essary steps to obtain. hWat more.csn be said than this, . that we shall get them as early as possible ? Mr. B. says in the last paragraph but one that this power can be obtained in 6 months' time. Of all the injudicious observations this is the most, and clearly indicates though he isknown as an able man t list he has yet much to learn as to how an Act of Parliament is obtained by a Corporation. 1 said that it would he the middle of 1893 before we can get our Act. 1 repeat it, and I will prove it, and in provinc, it I shall have at the same time to make it clear that Mr. B. is altogether wrong when be says there is no occasion .lo wait, that an act can be got at once,audthe whole business settled insix mouths' time.

A Corporation can only go to Parliament after compliance with certain forms, and after obtaining authority f coin the ratepayers. The notice of their ;intention to apply has to be given spila sanction ob- tained during the month of October and ;Nov., and the-Bill deposited not later than the 20th December (for this information 1 am indebted to the Town Clerk). We can only deposit our Bill on or before the 20th Decembernext. It has then to pass its.ex- amitnition, get through the committee stage, and. finally through the House, and A have no hesitation in saying tins will take six months. The earliest moment therefore will of; 12 months from this ere our Bill bemomes an Act of l'arliameot. how much short of the Middle oh 1805 will Mr. B. tttll us that will be ?'' .

'The last paragraph of Mr.B's latest is another bold assumption which had he a larger equaintance with these matters he would never have Made. He therein states that a large sum of money can be saved if the Corporation consolidated the whole of their loans and paid it back upon a 60 years' scale. Really one would gather from his that• Mr. B be- lieves the council itself has power to fix the time in which we shall reoay ? Let me again assert we have to take what we can get,and as the latest illu- stration I would mention the loan of .f.:000 ob- tained during the recent coal strike for the purpose of forming and paving sundry streets. We ob- tained powers te borrow tnis money ' and 20 years only in which to repay it. "After whet 1 quoted in toy last,viz: the roolutions of the select committee of the liou-o of Commons, which, by the x% uy, are taken from the proceed- inge, of the House, it is most imprudent to suggest that we can get 60 years for ait our indeht,aineqs, and therefore the ti,lures upon which this is ba:•ed are fallacious in the highest degree.
"I must apologise to your readers for having to re- peat ti.es ."‘tatellitqlts and With Chi:: :A) far a 6 I am concerned the dizeusiiion must cease.

div.head: COLLAPSE OF A RAILWAY TUNNEL AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: COLLAPSE OF A RAILWAY TUNNEL AT ST. HELENS.

Between nine and ten o'clock on Tuesday night a por- tion of the tunnel which runs through Cropper's Hill, on the Ra*enhead mineral branch of the London and North- Western Railvray, about a mile from St. Helens Station, collapsed, and some property belonging to Mr. Penning- ton above it,sustained considerable damage. It appears that a young man was in the yard of the residence or Mr. Thomas, a miner, when he felt a movement of the ground under him. He got away as quickly as possible, and shortly afterwards there was a subsidence which ended in a deep aperture being left. A load of coal which was in the yard was engulfed, and the outhouses and walls were rendered unsafe. Information was con- veyed ta the railway authorities, and Mr. Price, of Wigan. assistant superintendent, Inspector Sandbach, and other railway officials, with a gang of men, wer:, soon on the spot. The line commences near the Stanley Inn at Peasley Cross, on the St. Helens and Whines line, and runs to the Eacleston Hall Colliery. No train was in the tunnel at the time of the collapse, and fortunately no one was injured.
•B.k.ICERS' DISPUTE AT ST. HELENS

A singular dispute-. has arisen •at the Hardshaw Mills Bakery, College-street; St. Helens, belonging to Mr. Lionel Swift. Several weeks ago the Si. Helens branch of the Operative Bakers' Association agitated for a reform in the times of starting work and for a uniform rate of wages, and their demands were granted. Mr.Swift,while agreeing to the times of start- ing, objected to the wages terms, and told the amion officials they could take their men out. 'Three men were employed, but they continued working until a fortnight ago, when the second hand was dischar.:ed by Mr.Swilt. Tnis appears to have annoyed the, union men, and the fore hand was brought out. Mr. Swift then employed non-union men, and on Sunday, about fifty bakers paraded College•st.in front of Mr. Swift's premises with a view to prevent the non-union men going to work. They did not stay in the neighbourhood very long,but about a dozen men remained all night as pickets. The men started work at three o'clock on Monday morning, but were protected, and no intimidation was attempted. On Monday night a number of bAkers paraded in the neigh- bourhood,and a crowd. largely _composed of women and children, assembled. awerat Constables were on duty, and nothing of a very rough nature took place.

div.head: NICE NAME FOR A SERIOUS OFFENCE.
div.p: A NICE NAME FOR A SERIOUS OFFENCE.

At Barnet Petty Sessions on Monday, Mitchinson William Latham Brown Latham, a Dunstable solicitor, and clerk to the justices for the .Luton division and to the borough justices, appeared in answer to a summons charging him with having wilfully given false informa- tion respecting the birth of a child. The proce&ings were instituted by the Registrar General. The defen- dant, a married man with a family, living at Dunstablc, had been keeping a separate establishment at Barnet, where he lived as the husband of a woman by whom he had had a child. He registered the child has beinf4 born in wedlock and the mother has being his lawful wife,and this was the false information complained of.. The de- fendant pleaded guilty to the offence, and counsel on his behalf, while expressing the defendant's dpep sense of the humiliating position in which he had placed himself, urged that it was not a case fcr the infliction of the maximum mimum penalty. Th 3 defewZant, lie said, was [Om- ated in what he did by a foolish sense of chivalry tm- wards the girl with whom he had taken up. The .uegis- lature distinguished betwa en false information tiven with felonious intent and similar information which wa, serious only to the extent that it was false. The defen- dant had broken the law, and did not wish to escape the strictly legal consequences, The Registrar General had but fulfilled a public duty in ordering the prosecution, but behind this waa . the personal spite of the girl's re- latives, and the defendant urged the Bench not to iin- pase a heavy fine, or one which would give ground for representations that the case was a grave one. me Bench, after retiring for consultation, imposed the maxi- mum penalty of ,23.0 and costs.

The sixth annual report of the Gas Department of the Warrington Corpcirati on has illSt been issued. In it the Gas Manager (Mr. W. S. Haddock) says : The gas buildings and manufacturing - plant have been kept in a geed- state of repair. The largest quan- tity of gas made In 24 hours at Longford was 756.100 cubic feet on November 9th, and at. The lareest q sent oanti'rout in 24 hours was 1,237,000 cubic feet on January 10th, and the smallest quantity sent out in 24 limns 1-94,400 cubic feet on Juoe 18th. The decreased make of gas is 4•37 per cent, upon last year's production. Alter our large increase in capital, caused by Ibe erection at Longford of a new gasholder, which works veer satisfactorily and will store 11 million cub: e feet of gas, thus enabling us to cope successfully with a much larcrer demand it is very disappointing to recerd the abovc.rdecreased .........option, which has been caused by an extraordinar. ~uny year (the fnest on record) and the prolonged coal stoppage. The larger capital costs us a,bont, i. and the decreased salas of gas about per 1,000 cubic, feet extra on the Corporation charges forlast year. TO ALL PEW-110 ',DEES. Sir,—Will you allow me to invite all pew-holders who may chance to see this letter to he in their places on Sunday evening next, %Jaen they will hear some profit- able words. The second lesson is taken from the Epistle of S. James who wrote as follows :—" If there come into your assembly a man with a gold ring in good apparel and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment, and ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, arid say unto him, "Sit thou itere in a good plaer," and say to the poor, " Stand thou here or sit here under my • footstool." Are ye not then partial in yourselves and are become judges of evil thoughts.? . . But ye have despised the poor. . . . If ye have respect to persons ye commit sin." The words are so familiar that they seem to have lost their power. and AA Canon Knox Little said at a public meeting at Birm- - ingliam, in October last, " The tiling that astonishes me about Christians is that they read the New Testament and then go and do things directly opposed to it." But who knows whether the text may net acquire a new meaning to some next Sunday. and proclaim in ia way not to be misunderstood "Thou art the rtian.'— Yours, etc., • H. CLABK.
Liverpool, June 4, 1894. It may inter(st some to know that June 10, will not again tail op a Sunday until 1900.
SUNDAY BANDS.

- you have drawn the attention of the public to the Volunteer band playieg in the Vicarage grounds here I would like to ask your readers and the Vicar how he reconciles it with the fourth commandment, which he reads in Church. Is he not breaking both the spirit and letter of this command, or the precept of Isaiah ? " If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbs.th from doing t hy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sahbatli a delight, the holy of the Lord, honouraNe ; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own waye,nor finding thine own pleasnre, nor speaking thine own words. Then shalt thou delight tt*self in the Lord ; and I will cause the.e to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the lien- tags of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath Fpoken it." Do the men who play (or rvon the bell- ringers) attend any service after so doing ? It not, why ? If not on account of the work involet,d, thenlet the work be stopped. Nonconformists and many church- people can find thetr wa to their respective places -worship without either bells or bands of music,—Yours truly,

MIL WILLIS AND THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC. bir,—Two voices out of "the church" have snoken - upon this subject through your paper—one declaring - that the traffic is a good thing sanctioned by the scrip- " turesand the example of Christ, the other holding the very opposite view. I will leave Messrs. Willis and • Reed to settle their differences, simply remarkiug that . when two euthorised teachers of religion differ so widely upon a question so eaey of solution as the drink traffic, one might naturally hesitate to accept their dictum re- garding more vital matters. liqu'ortraflic, as everybody knows comprises the M.eyhufacture and sale ;.of liquors whose essential and aeiowed function-la te intoxicate, mnre or less, according ..te; the quantity iiribibed. - And to produce these un- matural and unnecessary liquids, millions upon millions of tons ef grain designed for the support of human life •are every year absolutelfdestroyed in the Breweries and Ifllistilleries. We do not require the assistance of bishops, _priests, and deacons to enable us to form a sound can- zlusion touching the quality of this business. A fair amount of common sense coupled with intelligent and •::fnapartial rrnseryation will guide es to a safe and correct eceedict. if the liquor traffic- is a good tree it will Vroduce good truit Co be seen ain.l known of all men. Its AriegOs and supporter's declare that it does yield such fruit in abundance,l-mt they leave us in entireignorance as to where and whA it is. It is certainly not •to be found in the long hours and Sunday labour of the drink . malciog establishments ; nor in the sever . clays a week trade, and strife and uproar of the public-houses : the home life of the people is neither sweetened nor put ifir-d : by it; we cannot trace it in the dieorder which disgraces our streets by night as well as by day ; and sure I am that the churches and chapels are not benefited by it. There is no doubt, indeed, as to the vpiality and qi:autity of fruit in the shape of hard cash which •• the :rade" confers upon the drink makers and sellers; hut it ,i a terrible fact that every stride in advance made by the iquor baronets is accompanied by an increase in the poverty and stiffarines'of the.people. The good fruit of She liquor tree is not visible to cpinmotiobaervers, wid if it exists at all it must be'brily in-the imaginatiou of the traffickers and their fries. e - But, unfortunately for the peace and well-being of the .jeceierfrnu tate , therie is a superabuedance of evidence to t.pirove, beyond doubtetbat the (Beek tree is a bad one. .-"-Bv their fruits ye shall knoW them." Is there a home • In the British Islands-that has* not suffered through drink! We have only to pass through the slums oroilr towns alkiel cities to be painfully impressed with the aw- ful character of this fruit seer, -tti the degradation and ruin d men, women and children in localities that are a leetekerace to our boasted civilization. What are the poor ejnlitipers that crowd our workhouses but living inelan- choly' fruit of the upas tree of drink! Our pr;sons, too, ~'•rlY.d to OVerilowing with criminals of ev,ry rank and • -.4agee bear terrible evidence av,ainst it. Even in rural •evillasea the quiet life of the ceuntryes outraged by riot - ;SO debauchery at the villae.e.,e*plibbe." Every year `-i'lliens of money ere expended le tins country for religi- por.poses, hut I_ t hi nk tire most ent'. eFeaet ic religirarest will haledli-Artre to-sny that the rothlts are •Hatisfactorv. And why? BecansP,_ according to an eminent brewer, the late Charles Buxton, "the struggle of the school, the church, and the librarv.agairist the gin palace and th- beerhouse is only another development olthe war between • heaven and hell.'' Mr. Willis may rest aastired that his church and missions will ee barren indeed i•r; long as his publican friends and patrons continue to flourish. ours truly, OBSERVER.

Sir,—Oee is sometimes uncertain whether it v.-ere best to laugh with the " laeghine philrsopher " at tile billies feeiees of our kind.er o regard theta moreserieusly with the other one, who was dubbed the " crying philo- sopher." Wtherte, when regarding the Sacialiar, delu- sion. I have followed Deinecritus, and laughed abundantly at the vanities end vagaries of the faddists who would almost persuade us that the adoption if their panacea would transform the very face of nature. Certainly there is one nature that must be transformed ere Socialism can be a success ; human nature must be radically changed before that takes place. nut now, although still inclined to treat the matter as would Democritus. still our quondam fellow ,townf,man " comes in such a questionable sliepe," and, assumes so grave an air over the matter, that I will endeavour to keep my face straight and reply to the only bit of his letter which secres tO me to call for an answer. Mr. Ayteteaen says," Lot us ask Mr. Peers a qeeetion sug- gested by his own writines. Will he kindly tell us what nthereaUSPS outeide of "individualism and competition " is "largely con•ributive to the serious evils we see around us.?" The doctrine I have to preach is an old one, but a much—too much—neglected one; it is as rid • at least as Malthus. Over breeding is the cause—the main cause—of the serious evils we see around us. Go to Nature, 0 Socialist. study her ways and be wise. " Our universal mother, Neure," has a very effieient mode of settine this evil right when it occurs among her uncivilised children. When the mouths get too mane for the food available she reduces the number of mouths to the proper eaopoition for the available fowl. And at the same time and by the same means she prevents the too rapid increase of mere mouths ; iii ()niter words she limits the " output." Now man is an animal, and is largely subject to the same natural laws as the rest of animated nature.. But, by artificial means, man has placed 'himself beyond the operation of seine of the natural remedies for the evil of over-production 9ur:h as the medical preservation of (naturally) uselees lives. &e., fec..aed alerts artificial facilities towards superabundant antheecially)useless breeding. Now I am minded to think that it is a crime of scarcely less degree than murder to brig into the world children for whom there is no ap- parent place—eo quate means of suppoit. N:•xt to the taking of life, soeiery should set its face against this undue duplication of life to leave a bad world is surely not so ill a fate as to be unduly thrust into one in which you are not wanted and in wbicil you have to endure " the stings and arrows of outrageous fortune" for a weary liretime ! But the adoption of tho obvious preventative of this evil, aid progenitive of evik woullrequire the exerci,e of sell-restraint and self-sacrifice, on the part of the workers ; and mankind is ever readieet to seek the cause of evils outside themselves when in fact it is personal and peculiar to themselves. We should never have heard of 80<iia119ta1, had trade kept good and men had net felt the pinch ef the effects of their own neglect of above ieentioned salutary restraint. But no sooner is this - pinch felt than there arises the old outcry. •` 0 parlia- ment help lie l" and let us divide the goods and gains of othere in order to maintain the fruits exceemet. Stich in effct is the So eialist demand. The salutary self-restraint which is the remedy for the evils sought to he cured by Serialism is very unpopular, but the planting of the Secialistic mistletoe upon the Individualietic oak is quite agreeable to those who wish to follow to the full teeir natural instincts, while at the same time demurring to the punishment Nature inf Vets open them ter the indulgence, a big war—a pestdenee—or- this self-control would soon take t pith the Secialistin cry ; but the return of peep, city would again se men 'fereetting the cause of their re;eery, and laying the foundation for more.— Tonle Ac., JOHN PEWS.

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.
THE PARISH. COUNCILS BILL.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT WARRINGTON.

At the IVarringtou Town Hall on Friday, a corn- ' mittee of the Lancashire County Council held an inquiry for the purpose of making arrangements necessary for carrying into cifect the provisions of I the Local• Government Act, 1894, within the district ot the IVarrington Union. There were three chief points sc;*eduled for consideration mimely : The division of the district of the Haydock Local Board into wards; the division of any rural township into wards, for the election of parish councillors ; the number of parish councillors to be elected for each township entitled to a Parish Council. The Committee ccnsisted , of Messrs. V. K. Armitage (chairman),B. Grundv (vice- chairman),E. Guthrie,anct Mr.F. C. Hutton (clerk to the County Council). Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), and Mr. J. Logdin (borough surveyor), representA the Warrington Corporation; Mr. J. C. Sutton represented the Warrington Board of Guardians, and Mr. S. Sutton (clerk), and Mr. Wm. Owen (survevor), represented the Rural Sanitary Authority, and Mr. J. L. Tunstall, assist- , act overseer, represented the township. _

div.head: DIVISION OF El a I'Docr,.- INTO %ARDS.
div.p: DIVISION OF El a I'Docr,.- INTO %ARDS.

'The first matter brought before the Committetfor consideration was the proposed division of Hayclociilnto wards.—Mr. Ellis, solicitor, of Wigan, who represented the Ilaydock Local Board, said that Haydoek was framed into a Local Board district in the year 1873. The area of the district was 2,408 acres ; rateable value £20,616. and the present population 6,686. It was pro- posed to divlde the district into three wards, to be called the West, the Central, and the EaA-. The west ward would contain 278 acres, 411 houses, 2,496 inhabitants, and a ratealo!e value of .£?,755. The central ward would ,c,ntain 615 acres, 359 houses, 2,029 inhabitants, and £9,435 rateable value. The east ward would contain 1,515 acres. 383 howes, 2,161 inhabitants,and a rateable value of £3,426.—Mr. Jackson, overseer for Haydock, said that the proposed division would not entail any difficulty in the arramzing of the voters lists—The Chair- man a nnottneed that the memorial of the Board would be carried into effect. ORFORD AND LITTLE SANKEY. .
Mr. Helt-on said that a memorial hut been Tezeived

from the township meeting suggesting that the Jural parts of the township of Warrington should be divided into two districts, namely, Orford and Little Sankey.— Mr. J. C. Sutton said that the Guardians ha I ask:.d him to suggest that the hamlet of Orferd should be coupled with Winwick with [lnhale, to fbrin one separate dis- trict. —The Chairman : What do the ratepayers of the district think ?—Ma. J. L. Tunstall : The memorialists their expression of opinion at their last meeting.—The Chairman.: But do you not think the proposal of the Guardians would be received fovourably.—Mr. J. L. Tunstall : I have no doubt it would. But I cannot over- rule the resolution they have passed.—Mr. Hultnn said ha .uoderstood that there was to be an application to Parliament by the Warriegtan Corinration for power to extend their boundary and embrace something of the. district in question.—Mr. J. Lyon Whittle said he had received instructions to apply for Provisional Orders for thoseportions of the township lying to the South and south west to be added to thit borough which would em- brace Little Sankey and Arpley, and a portion of Latch- ford .—A fter a little further discussion it was decided to add the hamlet of Orford to the township of Winwick with Hulme, under the name of .Winwick with Hultne. The question of Little Sankey, including Arpley was next considered', and after explanations by Mr. J. C. Sutton and Mr. Whittle, it was decided to form a separ- ate district known as Little Sankey with Arpley, to be left for further treatment in cennectian with the exten- sion of the borough boundary. PARISI-I COUNCILLORS.

The fol/owing list of parish councillors for each of the townships was submitted by Mr. J. C. Sutton, and approved by the committee :—Burtonwood, 6 ; Cuerd- ley, 0; Houghton, Middleton. and Arbury, 0, Penketh, 7; Poulton-withiFt.arnhead,7 ; Rixton-with-Glazebrook, 7 ; Great Sinkey, 6 ; Southworth-with-Croft, 6 ; Win- with-Hulme, 6 ; Woolston-with-Martinscroft.,s. The representation of the extra municipal hamlet of Orford was included in that of Winwick-with-Hulme.

div.head: CHESHIRE TOWNSHIPS.
div.p: THE CHESHIRE TOWNSHIPS.

A Joint Committee of the Lancashire County Council and the Cheshire Coun'y Council -afterwards sat to inquire irita the C 3.80 cf the township of Latchford, which is partly .situated in the adminittrative County of Lancashire andVattly in the administrative County of Cheshire. Another subject for consideration was the numl-er of Guardian g and Rural District Councillors to be elected for each township. The same committee and officials were present with the addition Of the follow. ing gentlemen from the Cheshire County Council : Messrs. Lister, Bate, arid Harp. and Mr. R. Potts' clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Several members of the Warrington Town Council were present including the Mayor (Alderman E. Greenall). The Chairman at be outset explained that the Local Government Act nf 1894, divided automatically any district which was in the administrative district of two counties. It was.for them to adhere to such meaning ot the Act unless Some special .reasonswere given to thr Joint Ci;mmittee to persuade them to do otherwise. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle stated that the Warrington Cor- poration were anxious that Latchford should be con- solidated with Wallington and forth one entire township, ' to be co-extensive with the borough of Warrington. This was an arrangement which nem seemed to be no objection to by the official representatives of local autho- rities. The Guardians,•and the overseers, and assistant overseer (Mr. Tunstall held the office to Latchford and Warrington) were with the Council in this proposition. lie did not think it was necessary to adduce any turther arguments in this direction than to say the district was in communication with and formed a part of the tewn.and • also to draw the attention of the eommittee to the fol- lowing rec.mmendation which the Corporation approved of. and which emanated from the Ilaard of Gu rdia.ns : —" That co much of the parish of Latchford as is with- out the municipal borough be added to-such borcr-t,gh, so that the whole of such parish may be in one sanitary , district, And in one administrativi, county, or failing the Practica.bility of such addition, that such extra muni- cival part 19e a separate parish, and that in either case one guardian or rural district councillor be elected for same, and one guardian for Latchford Ward within the , borough." Mr. Milton said that the whole of Latchford was geographically stituated in the County of Cheshire.— Mr. Whittle said that was c?rtainly so,but it was chiefly in the admiristrativenounty of La ncashire.—Mr. Potts said that it was chiefly in the Parliamentary division of Attrincham -.The Chairman said this was the greatest difficulty they had to deal with.—Mr. W"ittle suggested that the question of administration was the chief On- ^sideration.—Mr. Hulton thought the most important point was thatthe owners in municipal part of Latch- ford would have to vote for the Altrinchatn The Chairman said this difficulty was a fatal one and he thought Latchford would have to rethain a separate township. After some further discussion it was decided' that the municipal 'part of Latchford shculd be consti; tilted a separate parish. Mr. Tunstall raised the question as to what would be- come.of the rural part of Latchford,. and ttP.! Committee decided that thisshnuld also form a Sepsratepirish tin4r tho name suggested by Mr. Whittle, Latchford With- out.

div.head: CHESHIRE TOWNSHIPS OF THE WARRINGTON
div.p: CHESHIRE TOWNSHIPS OF THE WARRINGTON
UNION.

The next question for. consideration was the advisi- hility or otherwise of separating from the Warrington Union the townships of Grappenhall, ThElwall, and Latchford Without.--Mr. J. C. Sutton said thatl the nearest Sanitary Authority to these townships was that of Lymm, and the nearest Union districts that of Altrin- charo and that of Roncorn. He did not think it praetic- ahlra or proper that the townships, which were now in the administration of the Warrington Union should be separated.—Councillor H. Robeas suggested that the prosent arrangement, should be allowed to continue. He contended that the associations and interests of the townships in question were entirely with Warrington, and there would be much inconvenience in coming into touch vitt) the administrative centres and officials of any other Union. div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1894.

'corn he wished to point out the great difficulty there would be in getting into touch with the administrative centre, and especially the inconvenience the poor people would experience in this direction. At present comma- ' nication could be affected with the Warrington Union by taking either is penny 'bus ride, or a twopenny train ride, and people could reach Warrington from the extreme end of Thelwall within A few minutes. If they had to go to Ditton Workhouse, they would have almost a day's journey besides having to incur considerable expense in. railway fares. (Hear, hear.) It had been argued that Grappenhall and Thelwail had once been connected with the Runcorn Union. That was so, but the Warrington Union had been compelled to take them over for the reasons he was adducing agaiest their being detached. Ile went on to state that the Union was formed in 1836 of 15 Lancashire township?. The Poor Law Board afterwards failing to induce the then Guar- dian% to accept from the Runcorn Union, Latchford, Grappenhall and Thelveall in Cheshire, obtained an Act enabling them to dissolve Poor Law Unions. The Uoion was under.thie Act compulsorily dissolved in 1845. A new Enion was next formed by transfer of Golborne and Kenyon to Leigh Union and by inclusion of the. three Cheehire perishes with Warrington Uttion. A Work- house at Newton and one at Warrington were discon- tinued, and, in 1851, a new Workhouse was built at Warrington (as ceetral). Separate homes and schoels or 200 children have since been built at Padeate (as entral). A lengthy discussion follewed and subsequently the Joint Committee adjourned to consider the matter in private. When they returned the Chairman announced that they had decided to include the townships of Grap- penhall, Thelwell.and Latchford Without in the district of the Runcorn Union.
THE CONSTITUTION OF THE BOARD OF GUAR-
DWB.

Mr. J. C. Sutton submitted a tabulated table dealing with the composition of the Board of Guardians, on the plan of one member breach parish, and one member for each ward. He proposed that there should be ten mem- bers for Warrington being nine for nine wards, and one for the district of Little Sankey with Arpiey. The remainder of the Board were allocated ;...A follows : Flay- dock 3 ; Newton 5; and on each to the following placeP: Burtonsvood, Cuerdley. Houghton, Middleton, and r- bury ; Penketh, Poulton with Fearnhead, Rixton with. Glazebrook, Great Sankey, Southworth with Croft, ' Winwick with Hulme, Woolston with Martinscroft,malt• ing a total of 23. Mr. Sutton said he believed it was intended to raise an objection to this list. He had been in consultation with the Town Clerk for some time, and even up to that morning he had understood that the Corporation of Warrington were in favour of his E cheme Within the last hour or so he had learned that they- intended opposing it. • Mr. Whittle said •he had been asked to oppose the ' scheme becanse it only gave Warrington what was con- sidered a very unfair reprmentation. There was a popu lalgon of 84,920 in the Warrington Union. and out of that number 52,742 were in Warrington. The rateable value of the Union was £354,005 and of thatWarrington supplied £l7, 400. They would see that this was plac- ing them at a great disvantage in comp,irson to the other wards and districts.

Mr. A. J. Jolley, as a member of the Board of Guar- dians opposed Mr. Sutton's scheme. He said it had only been adopted by a few members of the Board of Guar- dians and aas not a fair representati c n of their opnions Mr, William Houghton; Chairman of the Board)denied Mr. Jolley's assertion and said that he thought the sural districts had a right to a better representation,—Mr. Whittle proposed that Warrington should have 15 mem- bers of the Board, whilst Mr. A. J. Jolley proposed that they should have 18. Tho Town Clerk's proposal was strongly support,d by Councillor H. Roberts, and Coun- cillor Kennett, and Messrs. G. Ratcliffe; J. L. Tunstall, 3. Jackson (flaydo3kl and others. After a short privat3 consulation however, the Committee decided to adopt Mr. Sutton's proposal.
NEWION BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. A DISCUSSION ON TIIE POSTAL ARRANGE- M ENTS.

The umal monthly meeting of this Board was held on MUnday atternoon at the Town Hall, Earlestown. Mr. J. W. Emmett occupied the chair and there were also present : Messrs. G. P. McMahon, J. Smith, E. T. Evans, P. Thompson, T. Ormond, and R. Brierley .(surveyor.)
TM?, LAW CLERR'S HOLIDAYS:

Mr. Emmett Pxptained that the LAW Clerk's absence was due to his bemg. away on his holidays at lsarmouth. The Law Clerk had asked whe:her he should come to attend the meeting of the ,Board, but he (Mr. Emmett) had told him that it was not absolutely necessary for him to attend.
COLONEL MCCORQIJODALE.
A letter was read tr. an Colonel MaCorquodale stating that he was unll,le to attend the meeting as he was con- fined t.) his hou.e. FARLESTOWN'S POSTAL ARRANUEMFCNTS.

Mr. S. Walpsne on behalf of the Postmaster Genera wrote to the Chairman, informing him of the additiona postal facilities for Ea rlestown .which have ails atly• been published in the " Eleaminer." The letter boncluded by stating that careful enquiries having beensmade, it was found that the preseut; circumstances were not such as to wa,rrant the department hi: making Earlestown a separate post office as suggested in the latter portion of the letter from he Commissioners.—The Chairman said he theught manydf them had heard a great many com- plaints as to the new arrangements. It appeared to him from the complaists he had heard that the arrange- ments were anything but satisfactory. They Were not so good as they were before for several reasons. One Is ason was that they had merely given Earles:own a pillar-box. All the letters were now taken from the pillar boxes to , Newton. stooped at Newton,and PO3lO of them brought back again to-Earlestown to be delivered, which caused .14 hours delay; The bag, too, at the Earlestown - office was not able ti hold all, tile letters, and some fell into the passage. and Were liable to be lost. There was another thing -which e as very objectionable so far as the inhabi- tants of Earlestown were concerned, and that was that the let&n.sdicl not bear the Earlestown postmark, but the Newton postmark. Therefore, they were "'miffed out" as it ;sere, altogether. Ile thous7ht ten or tweive thousand inhatai:antsoid not want to be in that position. The mail bags,instead of being taken to Newton ,and some of them having to come past Earieesown station again, could be taken diiect from Earlestown poet office to thes station. Toe inhabitants were taking this matter up as well as the Commissioners, but he thought the petition of the inhabitants was to be sent to the Postmaster General, or he would not have signed it. He had since heard that it was to be sent to Mr. Rich, pestmaster, Liverpool, which made it appear that he as Chairman. of the Beard was acting in two. capacities. He, how- ever, proposed that the following appeal be sent to the Postmaster General " That owing to the unsatisfactory and irritating poatal arrangements which have recenV been made, and which practically place Earlestown in a much worse condition than formally, the Postmaster General be requested to order an independent and searching inquiry into the township's requirements. Such inquiry to be made through the Local Authority, and entirely apart from the local post office officials."— Mr. Ratcliffe seconded the proposition and said his letters now reached him an hour later than usual:—Mr. E.T.Evans supported.—Mr. Ormond in supporting the motion referred to the inconvenience caused to working people owing to their being unable to obtain a stamp after nine o'clock. He also spoke of the late delivery of letters, and said working people were now unable to look at their letters during the breaktast time, as they were not delivered until nine o'clock. He also com- plained of the irregular despatch of letters. He thought •the inhabitants in sending A petition. to Mr. Rich, were making a great mistake.—Mr. Smith was of the opinion that a deputation Should wait upon .Mr. Rich ; it Was no use writing letters. The letters were sometimes opened by a subordinate, and got thrown into the waste paper basket. He was quite sure that they would succeed far sooner by a deputation than by memorializing; He thought Earlestown was entitled to better postal faciii- ts.—The rkolution was amended to read "That the Chairman, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Oranand be a deputation to wait upon Mr. Rich to explain ,the unsatisfactory tal arrangements at Eirlestown and that if no redress be obtained from him, the Chairman be instructed to convey to the Postmaster General the resolution : That owing to the unsatisfactory and irritating postal arrange- ments which have recently been made, and which practically places Earlestown in .a clinch worse condition than formerly, the Postmaster General be requested to order an independent and searching inquiry into the Townships r,quirements. Such inquiry to be made through the Local Authority, and entirely apart from the local post office officials." This resolution was carried.

div.head: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

The annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of the British Women's Temperance Association, was held in the Co-operative Hall, Warringt,n, on Wednesday. A private meeting was held in the afternoon, over which Mrs..Shilston, presided, after which a tea was provided at which a goad number sat down.—At the evening meeting, Miss Bessie Dutton presided, and she was supported on the platform by Mrs. J. Yonge, Mrs. Emmett, and Mr.,. Sowerbutts. There was a fair number present. The meeting was opened by the singing of a hymn, after which Mrs. Gunnell, of.Penketh, engaged in prayer. . . . . .

Miss Dutton in addreSsing ihe meeting spoke of her hearers as comrades.for she said that they were engaged in the same good ,work, and were fellow workers in a great and glorious cause.' They must all remember that work was beneficial, for it was tilt the work 'that killed anyone, but it was the worry about the work. It was blessed to be engaged in noble work, and she was much struck with the book which appeared sometime ago called " Blessed be drudgery." What the world might call drudgery would he blessed by Gad, and labour had been sanctified by Jesus Christ. They must all remember that the principal work in any causa was done by the rank and file. The success of an army did not depend very much upon the officers, but it was the rank and file which did most of the work. There was a great deal in the temperance work to make them feel their helplessness, but they must always look to Him for the necessary light and hle3Bing. Recently, there had been a good deal of correspondence in the papers about the drink quesion, and there had been a great controv- ersy between one or two of their, public men. The Rector said something which some took exception to, and others wrote in support of his views. They had had a noble letter from one of the clergymen, in which he said that the question was one to he approached in a epirit of self-sacrifice. It was a question of how much their influence would extend to other people. She was speaking that night mostly to abstainers, but if there should be anyone who' was not a total abstainer, she would ask them to help them in their cause. It was a ()Teat disappointment that the Government had felt itself compelled to abandon the. Veto Bill. %%bat could he more of a disappointment to them, when they looked at political life, and found thst the bill had been forced to give way to other things which they felt were infin- itely less important and less desirable. But let them continue to' work and not be discouraged, and victory would finally be theirs. She appealed to the Warrirwt-m Women's Temperance Association to speak out in no uncertain sound. -

, • , Mrs. EMMETT. of Leeds, next addressed the meeting. She said that she was delighted with the preamble of the ! British Women' Temperance Association, which began thus :"We of the British Women's Temperance Asso- ciation in the spirit of Christ, for the love of God, and the uplifting of humanity, hind ourselves tefgether." That was just what they believed in. They were work- ing for the uplifting of humanity,and believed that they had the blessing of God in their work. She had a noble ideal of womanhood. She believed that the women of the country could do a great deal for the world in this direction. It had been said that the place for Women was within the four corners of her house. That was slf course, her place, and her first place. But if she had time, then it was her duty to do all in her power to assist in the raising of her sisters from the misery which was so rampant in the world. She herself gloried in the work, and since April of last year, she had travelled 10,000 miles in Great Britain alone, besides 12,000 with Lady Henry Somerset in America, and had delivered 323 addresses in that time. It was a melancholy thing that they had a Government bringingin a measure for the control of the "rink traffic, and which found it had not sufficient backing in the present House of Commons to Pass that measure into law, and so the measure had to he laid aside. This bill only gave the peor man the same power that at present the landlord enjoyed. Mr. Walter Mactaren had been championing the cause of woman, and she had a resolution to propose that night which would support his action in the House of Corn- mops. She wag sure that if the vote was grant ,u 1 to the women, that their vote would go in favour of temper- ance, and it was for that reason that she supported the movement for women's suffrage. • When the Budget was done with, the Registration Bill would be dealt with, mkt Mr. Walter MeLaren had obtained the information from the Speaker, that he would he in order to move an instruction to allow " all ratepayers " to have Parlia- mentary votes. If this instruction was carried,it would allow all women ratepayers to exercise their vote. Mrs. Emmett then proceeded to give some of her experiencei in America, where she went in company with Lady Henry Somerset., as a delegate from Great Britain to the conference of the World's Women's Temperance Associa- tion. She inentinned the fact of the state of Ohio, and the province of Ontario !-leie4 prohibition states,and said that she thrmeht that Eagland showed a bad example to her datieditere, as the public houses were even open on Sundays in thia country. She concluded her address by moving the following resolution : " That this meeting strongly urges upon the Government, as the Registra- tion Bill which it has recently introduced alters the qualification for the Parliamentary:vote,in resriect to rat- ing and residence, it should also alter the qualification in respect to sex, and this meeting rejoices to learn that an effort will he made to include provisions for the enfran- chisement of women, and it hereby resolves to urge upon every Liberal, Conservative, Unionist, and Nation- alist Member of Parliament to support any instruction or amendment necessary for this purpose, and orders a copy of this resolution to he sent to every said member, and a petition in terms thereof to be signed by the presi- dent on behalf of the meeting. The resolution was seconded by Mrs. Sowerhutts of Liverpool, and passed unanimously, and the mee ting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

Loci. 13oArtn.—A meeting of the Lymm Local Board was held at,..the Boardroom, on Tuesday evening, when there were present—Mr. J. Gregson (in the chair), and Messrs. W. Brazendale, R. Whitelegge. Rouse (captain of the fire rigade).—The Law Clerk read the minutes of a com- mittee meeting,when it was unanimously decided to for- ward a vote of condolence to the widow of the late Mr. Cameron. The minutes were passed, and subsequently a letter was read from Mrs.Ca moron acknowledging the vote, and thanking the lioard.—Dr.Fox, medical officer, said that he attended the meeting for the purpose of recommendiiiir, that a freer use of disinfectants be al- lowed in the village. Ho believed they would Pe a pre- ventative against disease, and strongly urged that the matter be attended to, as all sanitary authorities con- sidered the matter very important. He had also to re- port that the village was singularly free from infectious disease. That was satiafactory, hut the horrible-music that was allowed to be played in Lvinm during the hrli- days was riot satisfactory. It drove him out of the Place, and he thought the matter ought to be attended to. With regard to the question of disinfecting the grids in the village, the Surveyor was requested to see to the matter.—The Gas Manager reported that th production. of gas during the nast month had been 692,000 cubic feet against .675,500 cubic feet during the previous month.—The report was adopted,and this concluded the business.

In the House of .Commons on Thursday evening, Mr Fowler replying to a question put by Mr. Knatchbull- Hugessen, protested against the suggestion that the smearing of mango trees in India was connected with the action of the Giwermiient in regard to the cadastral survey, and said questions of this kind were not calcu- lated to assist good government in that country. Sir W. tiAncomer informed Mr. W. Redmond that he should he most anxious to consider with the greatest ; care and respect any recommendation which the colonies might make in rega.rd to the proposed estate duties. In reply to Mr. r. W. Russell the right hon. gentleman said the omission of the Local Veto Bill trim the order hook of the House was an accident, and the bill would apnear on the orders on Friday. The House went into committee again on the Budget Bill. • The debate was adjourned at midnight.
FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. J. REY- NOLDS, LP.

div.head: IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY.
div.p: IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY.

The little village of Helsby presented an ex- tremely mournful appearance on Saturday after- noon, when the body of the late Mr. J. Reynolds, j.P., of Fox Hill, was laid in its lat;t resting place in the churchyard. The remains of the deceased gentleman were removed from Fox Hill on Friday and borne by the following persons to the church ;—Messrs. John Dallimore, George Bowyer,George Lee, Ed.Moores, Herbert Lee, Thomas Hopley„John Thomas Garner, Joseph Heaton, Hebert Baxter, Thomas Tudor, Edward Bazley, Hugh Turner, Charles Bate, Joseph Ainsworth, William Cowap, L. Antrrqbus, Wilfred Priestner, A. Priestner, Richard Helsby, Philip Priestne.r, George Pea- cock, James Fletcher, Joseph Leach, and N. Griffiths. ! Some of these are servants at the Hall, others tenants, and the remainder members of the Sunday school class which Mr. Reynolds had superin- . tended for many yeses. The Rev. T. W. Vale, vicar, accompanied by the church choir, met the procession of mourners at the church gate and read the oening sen- tences of the Church of England burial service. Them- tenor of the sacred building was filled with people when the mourners entered the church. The service was con- tinued in a most impressive manner, the congregation participating in the sicging of hymns which had been specially chosen by the deceased before his death. The presiding minister sutKequently delivered an address, after which the service was concluded, and the body remained in the church until the following day at noon -when .a large congregation again assembled. This service was conducted by the. Revs. T. W. Vale and LLB. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham. Subsequently the coffin which was of polished oak, with brass mountings, was conveyed to the graveside by Messrs. John Dallitnore, George Bnwyer, George Lee, Edward Moores, Herbert Lee, and Thomas Holey (servants). On the lid was a massive brass shield bear- ing the inscription :—" James Reynolds, born Novem- ber 20:h, 1824, died My 30th, 1894." The burial cere- mony was witnessed by a vast assembly amongst whom were—Mr. P. Hutchings and Mr. J.)lan Hutchings (nephews), Mr. and Mrs. Charles Reynolds, J P., Mr. H. Reynolds, J.P. (Norton). Mr. James Reynolds (Warring- ton), Mr. A. Sylvanus Reyncids (Latchford), Mr. John Brundrit, J.P. (Runcorn), Mr. T. Baxter, C.C. (Dutton Hall), Mr. E. Wynne Jones (Dareshury H dl), Mr. R. White (Hale Bank). Dr. Bryant. the deceased'A•medi- cal attendant, Mr. G.L. Davies, J.P., Colonel Ashton,Dr. Steele,J.P.,Mr.J.H. Fleming, J.P.,Warrington,Mt. Lewis Voisey, J.P., C.C., Warrington' in addition to many other professional gentlemen from Liverpool, Chestcr, Frodsham and Warrington. Innumerable wreaths were contributed, some of which were exceptionally beauti- ful. Messrs.J.and W. Duttornof Warrington discharged the duties of undertakers with efficiency.

div.head: REFLRFNCE AT THE HELSBY ',Arum CHURCH.
div.p: REFLRFNCE AT THE HELSBY ',Arum CHURCH.

On Sunday morning, the Rev..T. W. Vale, Vicar of flelsby, made a kindly reference to the recent depar- ture from life of Mr. James Reynolds. The rev. gentlemen described the deceased as having been " thorough straightforward manly English gentleman," with no reserve about him. The Vicar went on to say that their departed friend had loft them a legacy by his example, and expressed a hope that it would be followed.

div.head: REFERENCE FROM Tux RUNCORN MAGISTERIAL BENCH.
div.p: REFERENCE FROM Tux RUNCORN MAGISTERIAL BENCH.

Previous to beginning the ordinary business of the Petty Sessions at Runcorn on Monday rnorning,Mr. John Brundrit observed that he felt called upon to refer to the death of one of their colleagues who had occupied a pro- minent position on that bean for more than fourteen 'years. The late Mr. James Reynold, of Fox Hill, had perhaps been better than ordinarily qualified for the position of magistrate owing to • his honesty of purpose and integrity of mind, and had always dis- charged his duties in a manner appreciated by all right minded people. Tho same characteristics which had guided him al magistrate, were foil-wed by him in business, and there were few men held in such high esteem in commercial circles as their dep‘rt..d friend. He (the chairman) had lost a dear and a. sincere per- sonal friend, and he was convinced that the sympathy of all who knew him would go out to his son owing widow and family, who had sustained an irreparaVe loss.
_ Mr. Burton fully endorsed, on behalf of the legal gentlemen who attended the court from time to time, the remarks that had fallen from the lips of the Chair- man.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE FATALITY TO A SHIP CANAL EMPLOYE AT
WARRINGTON.

Mr. Brighous9, coroner, held an inquest at the Infix': mary at Warrington on Monday touching the death of Martin Burns, 29 years of age, of 13, King-st., Runcorn, a labourer employed by the Ship Canal Company at Arpley, who died at the Infirmary on Friday front in- juries received on the previous Monday by being crushed between a waggon and the tank of a crane. Mr. New- man, solicitor, and Mr. Davenport, agent, watched the proceedings on behalf of the Ship Canal Cornoany.—Lily Mary Burns, widow of deceased, stated that she last saw her husband alive on the previous Monday at ten minutes past four in the afternoon.—Nurse Dobson testi- fied to deceased having been admitted to the Infirmary at eleven o'clock on. Monday night suffering from severe injuries to the chest. He died at 12.40 on , Friday.— Frederick Wright, the man in charge of the steam crane erected at Arpley on a jetty, said there was a barge ly- ing in the river by the side of the jetty, and on the rail- way on the other side of the jetty there were some waggons. The crane was used to lift the empty wag- gons on to the barge, and the full ones on to the railway. Deceased's bUSiTWAS was to check the waggons and see that the boats were moored in the right position. While doing his work he could st and clear of everything, and had no business in the place where he was found.— Samuel. Cartwright said he was engaged in signalling for the crane to be manipulated. After he had signalled for the crane to be swung round en to the waggon, his at- tention was called to the tact that deceased was under- neath it. He had no business there, and had probably been " larking " with somebody below.—John Ea.som, captain of the barge, gave evidence to the same effect. —A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.

Sr. lisr.Ess.—This match ..was played at. St. Helens on Saturday, and resulted in favour of Penketh hv an innings and 34 runs. Cowley batted first, but. Wareing and Aldridge bowled so well tnat they were all dismissed for 43 runs. Penketh scored 133.—Linney 71, Charnock 20, Sutton 21, being the chief performers. THE WAY TO SPREAD SMALL-PDX. FRICTION BETWEEN LOCAL AUTHORITIES. Owing it is said, to" some friction between local au- thorities," a tramping tailor named M'Clay, suffering from small-pox, was allowed to leave Rawtensta.ll on Tuesday night. He walked through several places in the Rossendale Valley, calling at public houses on the way, and was only taken in charge by a policeman at Burnley on Wednesday evening. Indignation and un- easiness are naturally felt in Burnley regarding the affair and a Local Government Boatd inspectOr has been or- dered to make an inquiry into the matter. A FIGHT ON THE FOOTPLATE. EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR. A remarkable case was heard at LangtoWn on Thurs- • day. George Glendenning,a stoker on the North British Railway, summoned John Blythe, an engine driver, for assault, and Blythe had tlken out a cross•summons against Glegidenning for a similar offence. The two men were in charge of a passenger train to Carlisle. They quarrelled, and while the engine was running at a speed of thirty miles an hour they fought on the fOotplate. Glendenning said Blythe knocked him to the engine floor and battered his head against the lever. On the other hand, Blythe maintained that Glendenning was the aggressor. The magistrates, after commenting on this new peril to pv,.sengers,adjourned the cases till next month for the production of additional evidence. Both men have been temno?rarily suspended from the service of the Railway Company. IMPERIAL PA RLIAMENT.
